_README: Waypoint notes, round 2: document-pointers and database bookkeeping the first pass could not see.

Round 1 used a deny-list of site names and found 75 notes. This used the object rule - a DOCUMENT is a source, PEOPLE are not - and found MORE. A narrower scan returns a shorter list, which reads as less work rather than as a miss.

Kept deliberately: map LABELS ("marked as X on the USGS topo" tells a climber what their own map shows), the land manager (NPS/USFS), pointers to our OWN beta, every climber name and date, and every admission that a pin is estimated rather than surveyed.

waypoints.name: Rachel Lake Trailhead
waypoints.note: Trail #1313 start off FR 4930; Northwest Forest Pass plus self-issued wilderness permit required (USFS Rachel Lake Trailhead page).
waypoints.directions: From I-90 Exit 62, follow Kachess Lake Road to FS Road 4930 and drive it to the road end at about 2,800 ft. Trail #1313 leaves the parking area; a Northwest Forest Pass plus a self-issued wilderness permit are required at the board.

waypoints.name: Rachel Lake
waypoints.note: ~4.1 mi from the trailhead, at the top of the steep, rooty 'mile from hell' climb.
waypoints.directions: Trail #1313 runs beside Box Canyon Creek on gentle grade for roughly 2.75 miles, crossing several side streams and cascades — water is reliable the whole way, so there is no need to carry much from the car. Past the creek crossing the trail turns into the rooty, rocky boot-beaten climb locals call the 'mile from hell': about 1,300 ft of gain in a mile with large step-ups and no switchbacks. It is a fitness crux, not a technical one, but it is brutal under a full pack.

waypoints.name: Rampart Ridge / Rampart Lakes junction
waypoints.note: Ridge crest above Rachel Lake where the maintained trail splits toward Rampart Lakes and Lila Lake. Coordinate is a trail-guide interpolation (no exact published fix found), cross-checked against a nearby Rampart Lakes basin waypoint at 47.4182,-121.3376.
waypoints.directions: At the lake a use path branches off near the outhouse and skirts the north shore. From there it switchbacks steeply up rocky tread for about half a mile to the crest of Rampart Ridge, where the maintained trail splits toward Rampart Lakes and toward Lila Lake.

waypoints.name: Saddle below Alta's south ridge
waypoints.note: Top of the boulder gully on Rampart Ridge; start of the unmarked climbers' path toward the summit. Coordinate is a geometric interpolation (elevation-scaled) between the ridge junction and the summit; no source publishes an exact fix for this specific saddle.
waypoints.directions: Stay on maintained tread through the Rampart Lakes basin, keeping to the east side of the lakes — the alpine turf here is fragile and short-cut social trails are deliberately blocked with sticks and rock piles. At the far end of the lakes, find the base of a large boulder gully with cliff bands along its left side and follow the boot path up it to the broad saddle on the ridge crest. The gully is loose enough that parties should climb it one at a time.

waypoints.name: Alta Mountain summit
waypoints.note: Reached past several false summits along the exposed ridge crest.
waypoints.directions: From the saddle an unmarked climbers' path leaves the maintained trail at a cairn and follows the ridge crest toward the summit block. It starts steep, loose and shadeless with large steps, then eases onto a narrow crest with sustained exposure: expect several class 2-3 moves, at least one near-vertical step of six to eight feet with good holds, a short class 3 downclimb near the top, and three or more false summits before the real one. Do not attempt this stretch with snow on the crest or on wet rock — the path skirts a cliff edge and the fall consequences are serious. Helmets are worth wearing for the loose rock.

waypoints.name: Twin Lakes Trailhead
waypoints.note: Start of the High Pass Trail; Northwest Forest Pass required at the trailhead.
waypoints.directions: Drive Twin Lakes Road to its end at about 5,200 ft. The final miles are rough and deeply rutted, and many parties park short and walk them rather than risk the car. A Northwest Forest Pass is required; the signed High Pass Trail starts from the parking area.

waypoints.name: High Pass
waypoints.note: Leave the maintained trail here; drop and follow the climbers' path east/northeast toward the old Gargett Mine.
waypoints.directions: About a quarter mile up, the short spur to the Winchester Mountain lookout splits off — stay north on the High Pass Trail. It contours the west side of Winchester, dips through the minor saddle known as Low Pass with open views west to Tomyhoi, then climbs steadily to High Pass. This is maintained tread the whole way, roughly 750 ft of gain; Mount Baker comes into view south when you top out.

waypoints.name: Gargett Mine
waypoints.note: Old mine workings; last reliable water source until lingering snow patches high on the peak. Coordinate is the surveyed mine adit (elev 5708 ft) - parties camp in the basin just below at ~5400 ft.
waypoints.directions: Leave the maintained tread at the pass and follow the climbers' path east and northeast, dropping about 550 ft to the old mine workings. Tent space here is limited, so most parties bivy rather than camp properly. Fill up: the mine creek is the last easy water until lingering snow patches high on the peak.

waypoints.name: Notch (Mt. Larrabee NW rib)
waypoints.note: Reached after a long, unmarked sidehill traverse below Larrabee's southwest and west flanks; drop slightly beyond into the red talus/moraine bowl. Coordinate is a geometric interpolation (elevation-scaled) between Gargett Mine and the summit; no source publishes an exact fix for this notch.
waypoints.directions: From the mine, traverse north across Larrabee's timbered southwest rib in the first quarter mile, then commit to a full mile of unmarked sidehill below Larrabee's west flank — steep talus, scree, heather and slick herbaceous slopes with no tread. A small scree chute at the end leads to the notch in Larrabee's rocky northwest rib. Do not start this traverse on wet grass or wet rock; helmets go on here and stay on, since rockfall is the defining hazard of the whole approach.

waypoints.name: South AmBo Saddle
waypoints.note: Scrambling and low 5th-class climbing begins here, below the rock feature climbers call 'De Gaulle's Nose'. Coordinate is a geometric interpolation (elevation-scaled) between Gargett Mine and the summit; no source publishes an exact fix.
waypoints.directions: Beyond the notch, descend a steep dirt chute between snow and rock, then contour at roughly 5,800 ft above the moraine bowl. From there angle north through a series of steep gullies and ribs to the saddle. Route-finding, not difficulty, is what costs time on this section, and the red talus is loose throughout.

waypoints.name: American Border Peak summit
waypoints.note: Views to Mt. Larrabee, Canadian Border Peak, and the Pickets.
waypoints.directions: Follow a faint climbers' path along the crest for about two hundred yards, then traverse right onto slabby red ledges near a rock rib. A cleft just left of the rib and more slabby ledges gain a flat step on top of it; a down-sloping bench then crosses to the mouth of a steep snow gully, where a tall snow fin splits the gully and you take a moat on either side or the hole through the fin itself. From the notch above, three pitches of the Great Chimney lead to the top — a 5.3 entry, a smooth 5.4 face move over a large chockstone, and a squeeze so tight that packs have to be pushed through ahead of the climber. Above the chimney a dirty slabby trough, a row of horns and gaps, and one dramatically exposed step-across finish the climb.

waypoints.name: Watson Lakes Trailhead
waypoints.note: This is the Anderson and Watson Lakes trailhead, which serves the north-east side of the peak — the Green Lake Glacier and Watson Lakes approach — not the Diobsud Creek Glacier side this route is named for.

waypoints.name: Wilderness-boundary saddle
waypoints.note: Trail forks here — right drops 0.5mi to Lower Anderson Lake, left climbs into the Noisy-Diobsud Wilderness toward Watson Lakes.

waypoints.name: Watson Lakes
waypoints.note: Last reliable water and the only legal campsites before the cross-country push into Diobsud basin; designated sites only, campfires prohibited.

waypoints.name: Diobsud basin
waypoints.note: Off-trail descent from the Watson/Diobsud divide into the Diobsud Creek drainage; drop straight to the valley floor rather than contouring from the lakes, which is slower.

waypoints.name: Access gully to Diobsud Creek Glacier
waypoints.note: Loose rock and slick dirt in the chute leading to the glacier's toe once snow has melted out — expect to claw up steep, loose dirt gullies here.

waypoints.name: Diobsud Creek Glacier crossing
waypoints.note: Rope up here — crevasses open on the icecap by mid-to-late season; probe and stay roped through to the saddle below the summit block.

waypoints.name: Lower Maynard Burn Trailhead
waypoints.note: End of FR 2870-120 off Palo Alto Rd; Northwest Forest Pass required to park here.
waypoints.directions: Drive FR 2870 off Palo Alto Road to its end at the signed Baldy/Tyler Peak trailhead, a gravel pullout for about a dozen cars in the Upper Dungeness drainage of the Hood Canal Ranger District.

waypoints.name: Mueller Creek crossing
waypoints.note: Rock-hop crossing just past the trailhead; the rocks here are slick.
waypoints.directions: Follow the old roadbed a short distance from the lot; at about 0.3 mile the Baldy climbers' path (Lower Maynard Burn Trail #816) splits off to the right and begins climbing in earnest, and at roughly half a mile it crosses a decommissioned logging road. Mueller Creek parallels these early switchbacks and is the last dependable water on the mountain — top off here, especially late in the summer, since nothing above can be counted on.

waypoints.name: Maynard Burn fire-line clearing
waypoints.note: Flat clearing where the trail crosses an old decommissioned road/fire barrier; used as a camp before the steep push.
waypoints.directions: Steep switchbacks gain roughly 1,600 ft in under a mile. At about 1.3 miles the path crosses the old Maynard Burn track near a short junction with the Upper Dungeness Trail (#833.2), and continues above it as the Upper Maynard Burn Trail (#816.2).

waypoints.name: Eroded ravine section
waypoints.note: Steepest stretch of the climb -- crumbly, narrow (barely one-foot-wide) tread across a rocky ravine; the ~3,000 ft gain in the first 2 miles ends here.
waypoints.directions: This is the relentless section: narrow tread, in places barely a foot wide, sidehilling an eroding slope on loose dirt and gravel, with crumbly footing where it crosses the rocky ravine. By about two miles the forest thins and Tyler Peak comes into view.

waypoints.name: Ridge crest water source
waypoints.note: Trail tops out on the ridge crest with an accessible water source; exposed to frequent wind blasts.
waypoints.directions: Above the ravine the tread turns faint and muddy through boggy meadow benches where flagging and cairns are sparse, then breaks out onto the open ridge crest east of Baldy at roughly 2.7 miles. This is where the route leaves the trees for good and the first views north to the Strait of Juan de Fuca and Vancouver Island open up — fix the spot in your memory, because it is the key handrail on the way down in fog.

waypoints.name: Gray Wolf Ridge saddle
waypoints.note: Low point where the Baldy climbers' path joins Gray Wolf Ridge proper; Class 1-2 talus/ridge walking begins here.
waypoints.directions: A short step west along the crest ends the formal trail tread. Everything above is cross-country over talus and heather with no maintained path, fully exposed to wind and cloud.

waypoints.name: False summit (Pt. 6537)
waypoints.note: Marked as a separate high point on USGS maps -- traverse below it through open talus rather than over the top to save effort.
waypoints.directions: Continue west along the open crest on talus. In poor visibility this bump is routinely mistaken for the true top, and it is the spot people most often lose the line on the descent, so note how you pass it on the way up.

waypoints.name: Baldy summit
waypoints.note: True summit; 360-degree views of Mount Constance, the Strait of Juan de Fuca, and Vancouver Island.
waypoints.directions: A final few hundred feet of open ridge west from the bump reaches the true summit, which holds an old campsite. Lingering snow can bury the boot path through this section into June and the crest catches the full wind; carry a map or GPS track, since this is the stretch that causes trouble when cloud rolls in.

waypoints.name: Bacon Creek Road End
waypoints.note: Road-end parking off WA-20 near Bacon Creek (~MP 112); a 2018 rockslide near mile 4.7 limits the road to high-clearance vehicles beyond that point.
waypoints.directions: Bacon Creek Road leaves WA-20 near milepost 112 and runs up to a road-end parking spot at about 850 ft in the Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest. A 2018 rockslide near mile 4.7 limits the road to high-clearance vehicles beyond that point, and the drivable end shifts year to year with washouts, so a bad year simply adds road-walking to the front of the approach. Nothing is signed or maintained from the road end: the route continues on an intermittent boot path along the old roadbed before angling up onto Porkbelly Ridge.

waypoints.name: Porkbelly Ridge crest gain
waypoints.note: Off-trail bushwhack up onto Porkbelly Ridge, repeatedly described by climbers as one of the brushiest ridges in the range — no tread, slow going.

waypoints.name: Berdeen Lake
waypoints.note: Large alpine cirque lake beneath Berdeen Peak's NW slopes, often still substantially ice-covered into August; last reliable water before the high camp.

waypoints.name: High camp above Berdeen Lake
waypoints.note: Established high camp roughly 800 ft above Berdeen Lake, used as the base for the summit push; Day 1 totals 6.3 mi / 6,550 ft gain to this camp.

waypoints.name: East ridge gain point
waypoints.note: Leave the high camp and climb onto Berdeen Peak's east ridge, which the route follows before cutting onto the NW slopes near the top.

waypoints.name: Mossy Class 4 step
waypoints.note: One or two low Class 4 moves on mossy, heather-covered rock just below the summit block — greasy and exposed when wet or frosted.

waypoints.name: Berdeen Peak
waypoints.note: True summit (6,420 ft); descent reverses the ascent line back through the high camp and down the Porkbelly Ridge bushwhack.

waypoints.name: Buckskin Ridge Trailhead (Slate Pass)
waypoints.note: Self-issue wilderness permit and Northwest Forest Pass at the kiosk; trail #498 starts at the second switchback beyond the horse-loading area on Slate Peak Road.
waypoints.directions: FS-5400 runs about 20 miles of narrow gravel from Mazama up to Harts Pass, and the Slate Peak spur climbs a further 3.5 miles to the road end at roughly 6,900 ft — the highest drivable road in Washington. It is usually not snow-free until mid-to-late June, and parking at the top is limited.

waypoints.name: Whistler Cutoff / Middle Fork Pasayten Trail (478) junction
waypoints.note: 0.9 mi of Buckskin Ridge Trail then 3.1 mi of the Whistler Cutoff drop you into the Middle Fork Pasayten drainage here; go left/north up the Middle Fork Pasayten Trail.
waypoints.directions: The trail crosses the ridge crest and then a signed cut-off drops off it into the Pasayten drainage, losing about 1,600 ft to reach the valley trail. A longer alternative stays on the trail system and comes round to the same valley by way of Robinson Pass.

waypoints.name: Fred's Lake
waypoints.note: Established camp and reliable water 4.8 mi up the Middle Fork Pasayten Trail from the Whistler Cutoff junction; the usual first-night camp for Blackcap parties out of Slate Pass.
waypoints.directions: About five miles up-valley on trail #478, gaining a little over 1,200 ft. It is trail the whole way, but expect brush and storm blowdown in some years, and a cold, pushy river crossing during snowmelt. Most parties reach the lake in around five hours from the road and camp there.

waypoints.name: Rolo Pass
waypoints.note: Cross-country ridge-crest pass gained the next morning above Fred's Lake; drops you into the upper Eureka Creek drainage toward Shellrock Basin.
waypoints.directions: Climb east out of the lake basin onto the ridge crest, about 600 ft of gain, on the first morning out of camp. Lake Doris sits a short detour off the crest here.

waypoints.name: Shellrock Basin
waypoints.note: Meadow benches below Shellrock Pass; the standard base camp for Blackcap, Mt. Lago and Mt. Carru, and the target camp for this route.
waypoints.directions: Drop east off the pass into upper Eureka Creek — dependable water, but historically bridgeless and an awkward ford during snowmelt — then climb back out east into the basin below Shellrock Pass. Reckon on two and a half to three hours from Fred's Lake for the whole stretch.

waypoints.name: Col southwest of Shellrock Pass
waypoints.note: Cross-country saddle where the climb leaves the basin and turns onto Blackcap's east face; cairned in places but easy to lose in fog.
waypoints.directions: Climb from camp to Shellrock Pass and leave the trail there. Traverse south-southwest across the open grassy and rocky basin, staying beneath the cliff bands, to the foot of a talus slope, then work its left (east) edge south to the saddle just past where the cliffs end. This is a mile or so of genuine route-finding with 1,000-1,500 ft of gain and loss; a steep snowfield below the pass often lingers and is normally bypassed on the left, so carry an axe if snow is still in. Some parties instead follow the ridge crest itself southwest from the pass, which includes a true knife-edge stretch at Class 2-3.

waypoints.name: East face scree/talus slope
waypoints.note: Loose, unconsolidated scree and talus on the direct ascent line — space parties out to avoid kicking rock onto climbers below.
waypoints.directions: From the col turn up onto Blackcap's east face and climb it directly, gaining about 450 ft toward the northeast ridge. There is no path, and this same ground is markedly worse to descend than to climb.

waypoints.name: Blackcap Mountain summit
waypoints.note: Broad summit capped in dark hornfels/shale (the ridge's rock visibly changes color just below the top) with views to Mt. Lago, Carru and the Pickets.
waypoints.directions: Gain the northeast ridge, where the rock changes abruptly to dark hornfels and shale, and follow it to the top, staying on its left (south) side where the terrain allows. Easy Class 2-3 with loose rock and some exposure near the summit. Camp-to-summit and back runs about five to six hours.

waypoints.name: Alpental / Snow Lake Trailhead (I-90 Exit 52)
waypoints.note: multiple sources describe the Denny Creek Trail -> Hemlock Pass -> ridge -> SE talus field approach used specifically for this Southeast Slopes route.
waypoints.directions: Take I-90 to Exit 52, then follow Alpental Road to its end. Park at the Alpental day-use trailhead, at roughly 3,100 to 3,120 feet.

waypoints.name: Source Lake Trail junction
waypoints.note: Signed junction on Snow Lake Trail #1013; leave the main trail here and head toward Source Lake basin.

waypoints.name: Source Lake basin stream crossing
waypoints.note: Climbers' path fords the outlet stream draining Source Lake basin around 4,100 ft; last reliable water before the ascent gully, cairns mark the crossing.

waypoints.name: Gully 'secret passage' below the cliffs
waypoints.note: Trip-report landmark: an easy-to-miss rock passage at ~4,780 ft where the route leaves the open streambed gully and climbs NE along cliff bands into the upper basin.

waypoints.name: Thumbtack (rock tower), upper basin
waypoints.note: Prominent free-standing rock tower marking the talus basin between Bryant and Chair Peak; from here the route corkscrews southwest toward the Bryant-Chair gully.

waypoints.name: Bryant-Chair Peak gully / talus shoulder
waypoints.note: Steep, loose gully between the two peaks gains a talus shoulder on Bryant's ridge; helmets recommended, rockfall risk from parties above.

waypoints.name: Summit block traverse
waypoints.note: Route stays left (south) of the talus field and traverses the south side of the west shoulder before the final scramble; exposed with loose rock, though holds are generally good.

waypoints.name: Ross Dam Trailhead (SR-20 milepost 134)
waypoints.note: North Cascades NP wilderness permit required; a 0.6-mile spur trail drops to the Ross Lake shoreline where the multi-day approach to Castle Peak begins.
waypoints.directions: The trailhead is a pullout on SR-20 near milepost 138. A North Cascades National Park wilderness permit is required before you start.

waypoints.name: Ross Lake Dock / Boat Put-in
waypoints.note: Put-in for the Ross Lake Resort water taxi (or paddle) that shortcuts many miles of the East Bank Trail toward the Lightning Creek Trail.
waypoints.directions: A 0.6-mile spur trail drops from the pullout to the Ross Lake shoreline, losing about a hundred feet. Anyone bringing a private or inflatable boat portages it down this stretch.

waypoints.name: Lightning Creek Trail Junction
waypoints.note: Boat drop-off where the route leaves Ross Lake and picks up the Lightning Creek Trail heading east into the valley toward Freezeout Creek.
waypoints.directions: The lake crossing runs north to the Lightning Creek landing near the head of Ross Lake. The resort water taxi is the usual way across and books out well in advance; paddling it adds hours at both ends. Either way the return pickup is a fixed time, so plan the summit day around it — there is no quick walk-out from this side.

waypoints.name: Turner Bridge / Nightmare Camp
waypoints.note: Lightning Creek crossing near Nightmare Camp on an aging span; the bridge is unstable and a ford may be required.
waypoints.directions: From the landing follow the Lightning Creek Trail up-valley for roughly seven miles of forest walking. Parties commonly leave the shore before dawn to leave enough daylight for the ground above. The bridge is the Lightning Creek crossing and has been in poor shape; a ford may be the safer option, and that is a call worth making in daylight on the way in rather than by headlamp on the way out.

waypoints.name: Freezeout Creek Cabin
waypoints.note: Maintained backcountry cabin at the start of the abandoned Freezeout Creek Trail; the last reliably stocked shelter/water stop before the climb proper.
waypoints.directions: Cross Lightning Creek and pick up the old, unmaintained Freezeout Creek Trail. The first stretch above the junction is the trickiest route-finding on the whole approach: steep rock-and-alder slopes that take a rising, diagonal ascent line before you regain proper forest and tread. Flagging has marked it in recent seasons but do not plan on it being there. Back in the trees the tread is in decent shape the rest of the way, and the cabin sits just past a creek crossing.

waypoints.name: Freezeout Creek Ford & Blowdown Zone
waypoints.note: Trail disintegrates into heavy blowdown above the cabin; climbers ford Freezeout Creek and sidehill through alder to regain open talus near 5,000 ft.
waypoints.directions: About a quarter mile above the cabin, cross Freezeout Creek again and pass through an old burn. Tread mostly gives out near 4,200 ft where it turns north and re-crosses the creek, though the bushwhacking through here is not bad. Stay on the west side of the creek roughly 50-100 ft above the water — that band gives the most open going — until about 5,000 ft, where you cross to the south/east side and the ground opens into meadow and talus.

waypoints.name: Southwest Ridge Notch
waypoints.note: Gained via steep red heather and scree slopes; marks the start of the class 2-3 scramble along the SW ridge to the summit.
waypoints.directions: From the open ground above 5,000 ft it is a long, steady climb on steep red heather, talus and scree to the notch — around 2,500 ft of gain with no water on any of it, so fill from the creek before you leave it. Several similar-looking gullies and chutes feed this basin; note the exact one you come up, because taking the wrong one on the way down cliffs you out on bluffs well above the creek.

waypoints.name: Castle Peak Summit
waypoints.note: True summit, second-highest peak in the Hozomeen Range, about one mile south of the Canadian border; class 2-3 scrambling on the final pitch.
waypoints.directions: From the notch it is roughly 700 vertical feet along the ridge, mostly Class 2 with short Class 3 steps. The rock is generally good but there is loose talus on it, and the crest is fully exposed with nowhere to shelter — get off it early if storms are building. On this schedule most parties finish the descent in the dark, so carry headlamps regardless of the forecast.

waypoints.name: Alpental / Snow Lake Trailhead
waypoints.note: Self-serve day-use fee kiosk (Northwest Forest Pass or $5/day); trail departs the north end of the upper Alpental Ski Area parking lot.
waypoints.directions: From I-90 Exit 52, follow Alpental Road to its end and park in the upper Alpental lot (~3,100 ft). The trail leaves from the north end of the lot. Self-serve fee kiosk — Northwest Forest Pass or $5/day.

waypoints.name: Source Lake Trail junction
waypoints.note: Leave the maintained Snow Lake Trail here toward Source Lake and Chair's east basin.
waypoints.directions: The first half mile follows the old ski-area cat track before it becomes standard trail, then climbs gently through forest. Stay on the maintained Snow Lake Trail until the Source Lake fork — that is where you leave it.

waypoints.name: Thumb Tack
waypoints.note: Large rock landmark in Chair's east basin; skis or packs are often cached here before ascending toward the buttress.
waypoints.directions: Leave the maintained trail at the fork and continue cross-country on boot path toward the basin under Chair's east face, roughly half a mile to a mile of talus, heather and (early or mid season) snow. The Thumb Tack is the large rock landmark once you are in the basin; parties commonly cache skis or packs here.

waypoints.name: Buttress base / entry gully
waypoints.note: Blocky entry gully gains low-angle blocky rock leading toward the buttress prow; rope up here for sustained Class 5.6 climbing above.
waypoints.directions: From the Thumb Tack climb a short snow gully, about 300 ft, to gain the crest of the ridge that forms the Northeast Buttress. This gully sits under avalanche terrain coming off Chair and Snoqualmie Mountain and is a known early-season slide path — most parties carry axe and crampons from the basin onward and rope up at the base of the blocky entry gully.

waypoints.name: Tree cluster near buttress prow
waypoints.note: Notable stand of trees used as a belay stance on the ascent and as the first rappel anchor on the descent.
waypoints.directions: Follow the ridge crest up low-angle blocky rock from the entry gully to the stand of trees on the prow. This is the usual belay stance on the way up, and the first rappel anchor on the way down.

waypoints.name: Chair Peak summit
waypoints.note: True summit is the uncorniced center section with rock underneath; the northeast side is heavily corniced.
waypoints.directions: Continue up the buttress — four to five pitches of class 3-4 with big exposure. The true summit is the uncorniced centre section with rock underneath it; the northeast side is heavily corniced, so stay well back from the lip.

waypoints.name: Notch/saddle in main ridge
waypoints.note: Downclimb the SE-facing gully from the true summit to this notch before the rappels; steep unconsolidated snow up to about 70 degrees.
waypoints.directions: Descending: from the true summit, downclimb the southeast-facing gully to the notch in the main ridge. Steep unconsolidated snow, up to roughly 70 degrees.

waypoints.name: Fixed rappel anchor at rock buttress
waypoints.note: Double-rope rappel from a fixed anchor here down to the tree cluster, then continue rappelling and downclimbing to the base of the buttress.
waypoints.directions: From the notch, continue to the fixed anchor on the rock buttress. A double-rope rappel from here reaches the tree cluster, then keep rappelling and downclimbing to the base of the buttress and reverse the approach.

waypoints.name: Heliotrope Ridge Trailhead
waypoints.note: End of Glacier Creek Road (FR 39), 8 mi from Hwy 542; Northwest Forest Pass required for parking, self-issue Mt. Baker Wilderness permit at the kiosk.

waypoints.name: Climbers' Trail / Hogsback Ridge junction
waypoints.note: Fork just past the old Kulshan Cabin site; take the climbers' path right, up the Hogsback, toward the Coleman Glacier.

waypoints.name: Hogsback Camp
waypoints.note: Standard moraine-crest bivy at 6,000-6,200 ft used for both Coleman Glacier and Colfax north-face objectives.

waypoints.name: Coleman Glacier toward Colfax's north face
waypoints.note: Roped glacier travel across the Coleman toward the base of the face; watch for crevasses and serac fall from the icefall above.

waypoints.name: Bergschrund / mixed traverse
waypoints.note: Cross the bergschrund via a mixed rock-and-ice traverse to gain the base of the ice line, per route beta.

waypoints.name: Sustained AI4+ ice pitch
waypoints.note: A full ropelength of sustained steep ice leads up the line before the crux band.

waypoints.name: WI6 hanging ice curtain crux
waypoints.note: Free-hanging, rarely-formed ice dagger/curtain -- the route's defining pitch; only climbable in select conditions (formed only a handful of times per decade).

waypoints.name: Colfax Peak
waypoints.note: ~1,000 ft, 4-pitch line tops out near the true summit; descend via a series of V-thread rappels reversing the route, or traverse to the Colfax-Baker saddle.

waypoints.name: Rainy Pass / Lake Ann–Maple Pass Trailhead (Trail #740)
waypoints.note: South side of SR 20 at Rainy Pass, ~40-car lot with privy; Northwest Forest Pass required to park.
waypoints.directions: Drive SR-20 to Rainy Pass, about 52 miles east of Marblemount, and turn into the paved lot on the south side of the highway where the PCT crosses. Start on the Lake Ann/Maple Pass trail, which is well graded and heavily used the whole way to the pass.

waypoints.name: Lake Ann Trail junction
waypoints.note: Trail forks here — Lake Ann is 0.3 mi east while the Heather–Maple Pass Trail keeps climbing north/west toward Heather Pass.
waypoints.directions: A bit over a mile of gentle forest climbing brings you to the fork. Stay right on the Heather-Maple Pass trail; the left branch is the short spur down to the lake, which is worth the detour only because it is the last reliable on-trail water — fill here.

waypoints.name: Heather Pass
waypoints.note: High point of the maintained trail; leave the trail here and drop west off-trail toward Lewis Lake — can hold snow into July.
waypoints.directions: Two more miles of switchbacks through open heather meadow above the Lake Ann basin. This stretch faces north and holds snow later than the trail below it, so an ice axe earns its weight in June and early July when the tread disappears under snowfields.

waypoints.name: Lewis Lake larch bench
waypoints.note: Established camp on the larch bench above the lake's south shore; reliable water, but goats here are salt-habituated and bold around packs.
waypoints.directions: Leave the maintained trail at the pass and drop west off the far side on talus and lingering snow, then work around the south side of Lewis Lake to the larch bench above the shore. There is no maintained tread here, but a boot path is usually visible.

waypoints.name: Lewis Glacier / east moraine crossing
waypoints.note: Crampon up snow/glacier remnants on Corteo's north flank to the glacier's east lateral moraine; the glacier is retreating fast and late-season crevasse/moat gaps can open.
waypoints.directions: From the bench continue west across talus and snow, picking up the boot path onto the crest of the glacier's east lateral moraine near 6,400 ft. Early season this is a clean snow slope; by late summer expect bare ice, more exposed rock than the older descriptions imply, and moats where the snow has pulled back from the moraine.

waypoints.name: ~7,500 ft notch atop the moraine
waypoints.note: Gain the ridge crest here and traverse west toward a second notch; narrow, sand-covered ledges with exposure on this stretch.
waypoints.directions: Follow the moraine crest onto the snow and climb southeast, bearing left near the top to reach the notch on the ridge at about 7,500 ft. This is the decision point of the route: bearing right instead of left leads onto narrow, sand-covered ledges with severe exposure and a steep, constricted snow gully above — a substantially harder line that parties have ended up on by mistake.

waypoints.name: Second notch / cirque downclimb
waypoints.note: Downclimb from the second notch into Corteo's west-facing cirque below the Southwest Ridge; loose rock underfoot, stay alert for parties below.
waypoints.directions: From the first notch follow the ridge crest west to a second notch, then downclimb roughly 400 ft of dirt or snow into the cirque under the peak's west face. The ground is loose enough that anything dislodged runs the full length of the downclimb, so space the party out or move one at a time.

waypoints.name: Corteo Peak summit
waypoints.note: True summit (8,107 ft) topped via Class 3-4 scrambling up the Southwest Ridge; views across Ragged Ridge to Black Peak and Buckner.
waypoints.directions: Cross the cirque and climb the southwest ridge to the top on blocky Class 3 with a few Class 4 moves and real exposure in places; some parties put the rope on for the last section. Fix the notch you came down in your mind before you start up — the descent reverses this line and the notch is easy to lose from above.

waypoints.name: Stuart Lake Trailhead
waypoints.note: Self-issue day-use wilderness permit and NW Forest Pass required at the kiosk.

waypoints.name: Colchuck Lake
waypoints.note: Reliable water and camps; approach follows the same line as Backbone Ridge.

waypoints.name: Lateral moraine crest
waypoints.note: Traverse the lake's shore and gain the Colchuck Glacier's lateral moraine toward the base of the north face.

waypoints.name: Der Dihedral base area
waypoints.note: Route beta places the start near the Backbone Ridge toe below the Fin; detail on the exact line is sparse.

waypoints.name: Dragontail Peak summit
waypoints.note: Descend via Aasgard Pass back to Colchuck Lake.

waypoints.name: Hairpin Turn pullout (Hwy 20 roadside parking, Washington Pass)
waypoints.note: Roadside pullout at the highway's hairpin switchback just east of Washington Pass; no permit required. This coordinate is the one recorded for Hairpin Crags itself — parking at the hairpin is the entire approach instruction, and there is no separately surveyed parking pin distinct from the crag location.
waypoints.directions: Drive SR-20 to the roadside pullout at the highway's hairpin switchback just east of Washington Pass and park there; no permit is required. The pullout is the trailhead — from the car it is a short scramble up into the Ice Box, so there is no spur road or further driving.

waypoints.name: Ice Box right side topout
waypoints.note: Ice Box right side, Hairpin Crags, Washington Pass. The Ice Box left side crag lies nearby and is the one used by Iceman, Route C and Route D.

waypoints.name: Ice Box right side / Ephemeral base
Ice Box (right side) formation, Hairpin Crags
waypoints.note: Not a distinct mountain summit — a slab/gully rock formation that routes top out on. Elevation is an estimate carried over from the adjacent, similarly-elevationed Ice Box left side (5,490 ft); no separate elevation is recorded for the right side.

waypoints.name: Baker River Trailhead
waypoints.note: End of FR 1107022; Northwest Forest Pass required for day parking and a self-issue Noisy-Diobsud Wilderness permit is at the kiosk (confirm current FR 1107 access - a 2025 washout has intermittently closed the road at mile 4).
waypoints.directions: From Sedro-Woolley, follow SR 20 east 16 miles to milepost 82, turn north on Baker Lake Road (FR 11) for 14 miles to Baker Dam Road, cross the Upper Baker Dam, continue 8 miles on FR 1107, then turn onto spur FR 1107022 and follow it to the road-end trailhead. Pavement ends at Baker Dam Road; everything beyond it is gravel Forest Service road.

waypoints.name: Upper Watson Lake
waypoints.note: This pin is the lake itself, not the Hagan Mountain summit. Designated backcountry campsites on rock outcroppings along the upper lake with a privy; no campfires allowed - last reliable, easy water before the route goes cross-country.
waypoints.directions: Start on the maintained Anderson-Watson Lakes Trail 611 from the road end. Where the tread splits at about 4,700 ft, take the left (Watson) branch - the right fork drops half a mile to lower Anderson Lake - then climb roughly another half mile to the saddle near 4,800 ft where the trail crosses into the Noisy-Diobsud Wilderness, and descend from it to the lakes at about 4,400 ft. This is the last graded trail on the route; everything above the upper lake is cross-country.

waypoints.name: ~5,300-ft saddle below Mt. Watson
waypoints.note: Cross-country gain point beyond the maintained trail: traverse rock slabs, scree and lingering snowfields beneath Mt. Watson to top this saddle, then drop through heather toward the Diobsud basin.
waypoints.directions: Leave the maintained trail at the upper lake and go cross-country, climbing toward the terminal moraine below Mt. Watson. Traverse rock slabs, scree and lingering snowfields beneath the peak to top the roughly 5,300 ft saddle. There is no tread, no signage and no marked line from here on, so navigate deliberately with map and compass or GPS rather than expecting to follow anything.

waypoints.name: Uppermost Diobsud Lake
waypoints.note: Established rough camp in the upper Diobsud Lakes basin used as a staging point before continuing north toward the Bacon-Hagan saddle; roughly 6 hours of travel from the trailhead.
waypoints.directions: Drop off the saddle through open heather and easy slopes into the Diobsud basin, aiming for the uppermost pair of the four Diobsud Lakes. Heather and open ground with route-finding required, but no technical terrain. On-file timing puts this camp at roughly 6 to 6.5 hours and about 7.4 miles from the trailhead, with around 3,600 ft of gain and 500 ft of loss, and it is the standard base for the south-slopes climb.

waypoints.name: Hidden Lake (Bacon-Hagan saddle)
waypoints.note: Small unofficial-name tarn in the low saddle between Bacon Peak and Hagan Mountain, draining to Hidden Creek; reliable water and a flat-enough bivy if needed.

waypoints.name: Cliff-band forest slopes, south flank of Hagan
waypoints.note: Steep bushwhack north through timber past two cliff bands to break out onto open heather and grass on Hagan's south side - the most sustained brush/route-finding crux of the approach.
waypoints.directions: From the tarn, bushwhack north up steep forest, working through two distinct rock cliff bands - this is the sustained route-finding crux of the whole approach. Pick brushy ramps and weaknesses through each band to keep the ground climbable; above them the timber breaks out onto open heather and grass benches on Hagan's south flank around 6,000-6,400 ft, with seasonal snowmelt water and rough camps. Mark your line through the bands with photos, cairns or a GPS track before going higher: the descent reverses this exact ground, the weaknesses you threaded coming up are hard to spot from above, and the descent is consistently reported as slower and more error-prone than the climb.

waypoints.name: Scree/talus couloir col, SW end of Hagan
waypoints.note: Ascend a broad, loose scree-and-talus couloir to a col near the southwest end of the summit crags; this is the same col the descent down-climbs back to the heather benches - watch for rockfall onto parties below.
waypoints.directions: From the heather benches, ascend a broad talus-and-scree couloir to a col near the southwest end of the Hagan summit crags, around 7,000 ft. The couloir is loose the whole way - helmets on, and keep the party either tight together or well spread out rather than stacked, since anything kicked here runs straight onto whoever is below. This is the same col the descent downclimbs back to the benches.

waypoints.name: Hagan Mountain summit
waypoints.note: Class 2-3 scrambling up slabs from the col to the summit ridge; several rocky bumps along the crest, so identify the true high point before topping out.
waypoints.directions: From the col at the southwest end of the crags, make a rising, crevasse- and moat-aware traverse around the ice apron of the Hagan Glacier to reach the second col, the one between Hagan's twin summits. This short glacier section is the technical crux of the route despite the Class 2-3 billing: carry rope, harness and a crevasse-rescue kit, and put crampons on - on-file guidance recommends both even in midsummer, and although one published party crossed the upper glacier unroped, a single trip report is not the standard. The moat is the same hazard in both directions on the way back. From the twin-summit col a short Class 2-3 scramble on slabs gains the summit ridge. Hagan carries several rocky bumps of similar height along that crest, so identify the true high point (7,067-7,080 ft depending on source) before committing to the last moves.

waypoints.name: Lightning Creek boat landing / trail junction
waypoints.note: Water-taxi drop point on Ross Lake's east shore (~10 lake-miles north of Ross Dam); pick up the East Bank/Lightning Creek Trail here — this is mile ~16 of the SR-20 approach trail, a designated boat-in camp requiring a backcountry permit.

waypoints.name: Willow Lake
waypoints.note: Small lake along the trail (~mile 20); last reliable water before leaving the maintained trail — the 1988 southeast-buttress party left the trail just beyond Willow Lake to cut east toward the peak.

waypoints.name: Off-trail brush/ravine to the 5,000-ft shoulder
waypoints.note: Cross-country push through timber and avalanche debris into a deep ravine, then steep dirt-and-brush climbing to a broad timbered shoulder and meadows near 5,000 ft, bypassing cliff bands on their west side.

waypoints.name: 6,200-ft saddle below the SE buttress
waypoints.note: Ridge saddle directly beneath the southeast buttress, used as a bivouac by the 1988 first-ascent party; no reported water — carry up from Willow Lake.

waypoints.name: Southeast buttress — loose rock / crux chimney
waypoints.note: Divided buttress climbing on often loose, friable rock (hard hat mandatory, protection scarce); crux is a steep chimney (5.6) low on the buttress, followed by a 50° dihedral and a loose upper gully.

waypoints.name: Ross Dam Trailhead (SR-20) / East Bank Trail to Lightning Creek
waypoints.note: This is a long (~15+ mile) approach via the East Bank Trail, historically used for this specific technical route; most modern non-technical South Peak parties instead use the shorter Hozomeen Lake Trailhead at Hozomeen Campground (Silver-Skagit Road, from the Canadian side)

waypoints.name: Hannegan Pass Trailhead
waypoints.note: End of FR 32 (Ruth Creek Road), 5.3 mi off the Mt Baker Hwy; Northwest Forest Pass required to park, self-issue wilderness permit needed past the pass for overnight travel into North Cascades NP.

waypoints.name: Hannegan Pass
waypoints.note: Broad meadow pass on the Mt Baker Wilderness/park boundary ridge where the trail crests and then switchbacks steeply down into the Chilliwack River drainage.
waypoints.directions: Follow the Hannegan Pass Trail (#674) about 4.2 miles up the Ruth Creek valley, gaining roughly 1,900 ft through forest and avalanche meadows before switchbacks bring you to the pass.

waypoints.name: Boundary Camp
waypoints.note: First-night camp just inside the park boundary below the pass with a reliable stream for water; trail forks here toward the Chilliwack River/Copper Ridge.
waypoints.directions: From the pass the trail switchbacks steeply down the east side into the Chilliwack River drainage, losing about 1,250 ft in a mile to the camp just inside the park boundary. The stream at camp is reliable water.

waypoints.name: Chilliwack River crossing
waypoints.note: Ford (or cable/log crossing depending on season and bridge status) of the Chilliwack River; can run high, fast, and cold during snowmelt — check current NPS crossing status before counting on a bridge.
waypoints.directions: Continue down-valley on the Chilliwack River Trail, dropping about 1,500 ft over roughly five miles of forest past the Copper Creek and U.S. Cabin camps to the river. Bears have been persistent at camps in this drainage, so use hard-sided food storage anywhere you stop. Bring gloves for the hand-pulled cable car, and check current park crossing status before counting on it.

waypoints.name: Brush Creek Trail junction
waypoints.note: Leave the Chilliwack River Trail and turn up the Brush Creek Trail toward Whatcom Pass; junction is easy to miss in overgrown brush.
waypoints.directions: Cross the river and follow the trail about a mile up-valley past Indian Creek Camp to the signed Brush Creek junction, where the tread toward Whatcom Pass turns off. This stretch carries major blowdown from the 2021-22 fire damage, and the junction itself is easy to walk past when the brush is up.

waypoints.name: Graybeal Camp
waypoints.note: Established camp on Brush Creek that's often dry by late summer — fill water at the creek about half a mile before camp rather than counting on a source here.
waypoints.directions: Turn up the Brush Creek Trail and climb roughly 1,250 ft over about two miles toward Whatcom Pass, through the 2022 burn — expect rockfall off unstable burned switchbacks and falling snags overhead. Graybeal's own water source is often dry by late summer, so fill at the creek about half a mile below camp rather than counting on finding water at the site.

waypoints.name: Open slopes above Brush Creek (leave trail)
waypoints.note: Leave the maintained trail on the brushy avalanche-path slopes below Whatcom Pass and angle northwest toward Indian Mountain; no path from here, steep heather/slide-alder terrain with genuine route-finding as noted in route beta.
waypoints.directions: Stay on the Brush Creek Trail another mile and a half toward Whatcom Pass, then leave the maintained tread where the brushy avalanche paths open up below the pass. There is no path beyond this point, and the slide alder and steep heather make the route-finding genuinely sustained in both directions.

waypoints.name: Indian Mountain
waypoints.note: True summit; the peak drops over 4,100 ft to the Brush Creek/Indian Creek valley in roughly a mile, and hikers viewing it from the Whatcom Pass ridge describe an abrupt cliff on its north side above Indian Creek's headwaters — stay well back from that edge.
waypoints.directions: Climb cross-country up open heather, talus and short loose rock steps, gaining roughly 2,300 ft in about a mile and a half. Nothing here needs a rope, but the peak throws over 4,100 ft down to the valley in about a mile, so the ground stays steep the whole way and there is no quicker line down — the descent reverses this one. Near the top, stay well back from the north edge, which drops abruptly to the head of Indian Creek.

waypoints.name: Esmeralda Trailhead
waypoints.note: End of FR-9737 (9.6 mi up North Fork Teanaway Rd); free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the kiosk plus NW Forest Pass or $5/day fee for parking.
waypoints.directions: From I-90 exit 85 take SR-970 about seven miles and turn north onto the Teanaway Road, staying with it as it becomes the North Fork Teanaway Road and then FR-9737. Roughly the last ten miles are unpaved. The lot fills early on summer weekends, since this is also the main Mount Stuart access.

waypoints.name: Ingalls Way Trail #1390 / Esmeralda Basin Trail #1394 fork
waypoints.note: Signed split — bear right onto Ingalls Way Trail #1390; straight ahead continues into Esmeralda Basin, and dogs are not allowed past this fork toward Ingalls.
waypoints.directions: The trail runs north from the kiosk beside the creek on an old mining-road grade, gaining gently. The fork is signed and obvious; the Ingalls branch is the one that starts climbing away from the creek, while the other stays low into the basin.

waypoints.name: Longs Pass Trail #1229 junction
waypoints.note: Longs Pass Trail branches off to the right here; stay on Ingalls Way Trail #1390 (left/straight) toward Ingalls Pass.
waypoints.directions: About a mile of steady climbing on open slope above the creek. Longs Pass branches off here and climbs east toward Mount Stuart; stay left on Ingalls Way #1390 for the pass. This is the second junction of the day, not the fork near the trailhead.

waypoints.name: Ingalls Pass
waypoints.note: Broad crest with the first views of Mt. Stuart and the Ingalls peaks; trail forks toward Headlight Basin or drops northwest into the Lake Ingalls basin.
waypoints.directions: A mile and a half of steady switchbacks through open larch and subalpine slope, roughly a thousand feet of gain and no water anywhere on it. Snow and ice linger on the upper switchbacks into July in a heavy year, so microspikes and an axe earn their weight early season.

waypoints.name: Lake Ingalls
waypoints.note: Glacial tarn below the peaks with reliable water and scattered rough slab camps; the usual staging point for scramble/climb routes on Ingalls East Peak.
waypoints.directions: Cross the pass and drop slightly into the basin, following cairns and boot track around it rather than giving up elevation. The last stretch climbs a large, steep boulder field with hands-and-feet moves in places. Filter here — there is no water above the lake.

waypoints.name: North/East col chockstone gully
waypoints.note: Loose, chockstone-choked gully leading to the notch between East and North Ingalls Peaks; several sub-gullies exist and the largest, most direct one is the more dangerous line — confirm the correct chute before committing.
waypoints.directions: Pick up the climbers' path that skirts the east shore and head up-basin toward the obvious notch between the main summit and East Peak. Favour the clean granite slabs on the left over the chossy central gully, and at around 7,000 ft turn north into the gully system. Several sub-gullies go; the largest and most direct one is the loosest and is the one to avoid.

waypoints.name: Ingalls Peak — East Peak
waypoints.note: True summit gained by short low-5th-class slab climbing above the North/East col; descent uses three rappel stations down the Southwest Face (70m rope recommended) back to the col and Ingalls Pass.
waypoints.directions: Scramble the gully to the notch and the chockstone that marks the start of the climbing, with the belay ledge about fifteen feet above it. Two short pitches follow: slabs trending slightly left into a gully, then right onto the ridge crest to the top. There is a great deal of loose rock on that final stretch, so test holds and keep the party out of each other's fall line.

waypoints.name: Goodell Creek Trailhead
waypoints.note: Unmarked pullout off SR-20 behind a large boulder at Goodell Creek Campground; NPS wilderness permit required for overnight camping in the Terror/Crescent Creek basins.
waypoints.directions: Park at the Goodell Creek trailhead and group campground on SR-20, just west of Newhalem — an unmarked pullout behind a large boulder. If you plan to camp overnight in the Terror Creek or Crescent Creek basins, you'll need an NPS wilderness permit.

waypoints.name: Terror Basin climbers' path cairn
waypoints.note: Old roadbed ends and a rock cairn marks a hard right turnoff onto the steep, more-defined climbers' path, which runs atop a forested ridge here.
waypoints.directions: Walk the old streamside roadbed up the Goodell Creek valley at easy grades for about four miles, crossing the creek along the way. The last flowing water is near 1,600 ft and everything above is dry, so fill up there rather than counting on the basin. Watch the uphill side closely as you go: the turnoff is small, sometimes unmarked, and parties routinely stride past it and waste an hour on the valley trail.

waypoints.name: Terror Basin camp
waypoints.note: Glacial-outwash camping among streams below the Southern Pickets; treeline is passed around 5000-5200 ft on the way up.
waypoints.directions: The path goes straight up the forested hillside with no switchbacks and no let-up, a long haul on roots and dirt that most parties consider the hardest part of the whole approach. There is no water anywhere on it. Timber ends near 5,000-5,200 ft and the ground turns to meadow, slab and usually old snow, from where a rising traverse leads toward a broad saddle and the camping benches just below it.

waypoints.name: The Barrier crossing
waypoints.note: Loose, 'serious Class 3' rock rib separating Terror Basin from Crescent Creek Basin, just below Degenhardt; crossing higher avoids a longer traverse but involves a moat and low-5th-class moves — parties have turned back here.
waypoints.directions: Work up and across the basin toward Degenhardt to reach the rib. Where you cross it matters more than anything else on this leg — going in low is longer and brushier and has pulled parties onto fifth-class ground, while taking it high near the notch shortens the traverse but usually means dealing with a moat where the snow pulls back from the rock. The rock is loose enough throughout that a slip, not the technical grade, is the real hazard.

waypoints.name: Crescent Creek Basin camp
waypoints.note: Established camp under Mount Terror used as the staging basin for Inspiration Peak's west side; this is the 'Crescent Creek basin camp' referenced in the route beta.
waypoints.directions: From the notch at the top of the rib, drop onto the snow ramp running down the far side, which is an easy descent while it still holds snow and turns into loose talus and open moats as the season goes on. It puts you straight into the basin under Terror at around 6,200 ft.

waypoints.name: West Ridge gain point
waypoints.note: Leave the basin talus/snow and scramble onto the crest of Inspiration's west ridge above camp.
waypoints.directions: Climb the talus and snow out of the basin and cross the glacier below the peak; it is crevassed, and the moat or bergschrund at its head is the usual obstacle in getting onto rock at all. Start up the obvious gully above it and follow that until stepping out onto the crest makes sense, roughly 300 ft above the ice.

waypoints.name: Exposed gneiss ridge steps
waypoints.note: Sequence of exposed 5.7 steps on loose gneiss along the ridge crest below the summit block — the technical crux of the route.
waypoints.directions: The first pitches are the poorest rock on the route: slabby compact ground where anchors are awkward to arrange, a large corner and chimney stacked with loose blocks, and lichen-covered ledge systems leading back toward the crest. Quality improves steadily with every pitch gained. Belay somewhere out of the fall line of what the leader is going to pull off.

waypoints.name: Inspiration Peak
waypoints.note: True summit of Inspiration Peak in the Southern Pickets; descend by rappelling the west ridge crest with a single 60m rope back to the glacier above the moat.
waypoints.directions: Once the crest proper is underfoot the rock turns solid and well featured, and easy fifth class runs a couple of hundred feet to the base of the summit headwall. The last pitches take the headwall itself on good holds, passing a pale rock scar on the way to the top.

waypoints.name: Middle Fork footbridge
waypoints.note: Trail crosses to the south side of the Middle Fork Snoqualmie River on a footbridge; reliable water here.

waypoints.name: Hardscrabble Horse Camp
waypoints.note: Old road tread ends here at an established horse camp with views of rockslides and waterfalls; trail narrows beyond, crossing Hardscrabble Creek into the Alpine Lakes Wilderness just after.

waypoints.name: Pedro Camp / steel bridge
waypoints.note: Locally-known campsite where the trail crosses a steel bridge back over the Middle Fork; open avalanche-slope views of Burntboot Peak, Overcoat Peak and Iron Cap Mountain start from here.

waypoints.name: Williams Lake Trail junction
waypoints.note: Leave the Dutch Miller Gap Trail here and turn onto Williams Lake Trail 1030.1 for the 1-mile side trip up to the lake.

waypoints.name: Williams Lake
waypoints.note: Subalpine lake basin at the base of Bear's Breast Mountain; established campsites on the west shore, boot paths head up toward the high country from here.

waypoints.name: Williams Lake saddle
waypoints.note: Boot path gains this saddle above the lake; from here it's talus and boulder hopping onto the ridge leading toward the Iron Cap summit block.

waypoints.name: Dingford Creek Trailhead (Middle Fork Snoqualmie Road)
waypoints.note: approach via Trout Lake, Copper/Malachite Lake, and Chetwoot Lake/Iron Cap Lake basin to the peak's north/west ridge.

waypoints.name: Iron Peak Trailhead (Trail #1399)
waypoints.note: USFS trailhead on FR 9737, 0.5 mi past De Roux Campground; no fee/permit and no water or restrooms on site.

waypoints.name: Unnamed creek crossing
waypoints.note: Trail climbs alongside a steep unnamed creek for about the first eighth-mile before turning away from it for good — last reliable water, so carry what you need from here.
waypoints.directions: The tread pitches up the moment it leaves the lot — there is no flat warm-up — with the creek audible on your left through the trees for the first few hundred yards. Above the crossing the trail rides a rib between two drainages, which is why the water goes out of reach and stays there.

waypoints.name: Ridge crest / Eldorado Creek drainage
waypoints.note: Trail bumps over a minor ridge with Koppen Mountain and the Esmeralda Peaks in view, and Eldorado Creek becomes audible in the drainage below to the east.
waypoints.directions: Above the crossing the trail switchbacks steadily up a south-facing forested slope, gaining around 1,300 ft in a little over a mile. The switchbacks tighten and the tread turns rocky and uneven as the trees begin to thin. This aspect bakes on hot afternoons and there is no shade once you are out of the timber.

waypoints.name: Eldorado Pass (saddle)
waypoints.note: Broad saddle between Iron and Teanaway Peaks inside the Eldorado Research Natural Area (est. 1972); leave the maintained trail here and head north/right on the open ridge boot path for Iron Peak.
waypoints.directions: Stay on the maintained trail as it works up the ridge above the Eldorado Creek drainage at a steady moderate grade for another mile and a half. Snow lies across these upper slopes into late June and can bury the tread on the last open stretch below the saddle.

waypoints.name: Snow patches on the north ridge
waypoints.note: Lingering snow lingers on the open ridge above the pass into early summer; reported as easy to kick-step across but can hide the boot path in June.
waypoints.directions: The boot path climbs the open crest in the clear, on low brush and rock with nothing to obstruct the view of where you are going. It is faint in places, but the crest itself is the line — if you lose the tread, simply keep to the high ground.

waypoints.name: Iron Peak summit
waypoints.note: Broad open summit ridge-top (47°24'55"N 120°54'01"W) with views of Mount Stuart, Sherpa, Colchuck, Dragontail, and Little Annapurna.
waypoints.directions: The last half mile is open ridge walking on rocky ground and needs no scrambling. Stay on the crest rather than drifting onto the scree slopes falling away to the west, which are steeper, looser and slower than they look from above.

waypoints.name: Canyon Creek Trailhead
waypoints.note: Self-issue free Pasayten Wilderness permit at the trailhead register; $5 day-use/Northwest Forest Pass required for the SR-20 lot near Granite/Canyon Creek.
waypoints.directions: Park at the Canyon Creek Trailhead on SR-20, roughly 16 miles west of Rainy Pass at about 1,900 feet. The lot takes a $5 day-use fee or a Northwest Forest Pass, and there is a register at the trailhead where you self-issue the free Pasayten Wilderness permit. If you are camping, the high camps fall inside the North Cascades park complex and Ross Lake NRA backcountry, so arrange a wilderness camping permit before you leave. The route is usually climbed August into September.

waypoints.name: Jackita Ridge Trail / Crater Lake Trail fork
waypoints.note: Trail #738 switchbacks ~3,400 ft in 4 miles (about 55 switchbacks) to this fork; leave Jackita Ridge Trail and go left for Crater Lake.
waypoints.directions: Cross Canyon Creek on the log-and-plank crossing right at the start; it can wash out in high water, so check its condition before committing to the trip. Above it the trail settles into roughly fifty switchbacks and about 3,400 ft of forested climbing over four miles. Carry water from the creek, because the hillside above holds none.

waypoints.name: Crater Lake
waypoints.note: Grade flattens around 5,000 ft at the lake basin; campsites sit on the rocky south lip and the outlet is the last reliable water before cross-country travel toward Jerry Lakes.
waypoints.directions: Bear left at the fork and contour about a mile into the lake basin, losing a little height as the grade finally eases — the only downhill on the way in.

waypoints.name: Crater Mountain south saddle
waypoints.note: Cross-country ridge-gain point above Crater Lake where the trail ends and the route drops off-trail toward the Jerry Glacier remnant.
waypoints.directions: Pick the trail back up above the lake and grind out roughly 2,200 ft of long, hot, exposed switchbacks with no water on any of them. Somewhere around 6,700-7,200 ft leave the maintained tread and traverse off toward the gap between Crater Mountain's main summit and its east peak. Most parties are a little over four hours from the car when they reach it.

waypoints.name: Jerry Glacier crossing
waypoints.note: Small crevassed glacier below the saddle; rope up or wear crampons to descend safely toward Jerry Lakes.
waypoints.directions: From the saddle the route goes downhill onto the ice on the far side. Early in the season the glacier is snow-covered and crevassed enough to justify a rope and crampons; by late summer it is often patchy or nearly bare, which makes the crossing simpler but the consequences of a slide worse.

waypoints.name: Jerry Lakes / Crater Creek Meadows camp
waypoints.note: Established bench camp near Jerry Lakes reached roughly 8-8.5 hrs from the trailhead; standard bivy for a South Face summit push the next morning.
waypoints.directions: Continue down off the ice into the lakes basin, losing around 800 ft over heather, slabs and boulders with no set line to follow. Fill water at the lakes: this is the last of it before the face.

waypoints.name: Hidden chimney / red gully, South Face
waypoints.note: Class-3 hidden chimney cuts the lower cliff band above a fish-shaped snowfield and a slinged rappel boulder; loose rock, a short rappel, and exposed steep snow through here.
waypoints.directions: Traverse the heather shelf out of the basin and through the notch just south of the lakes, then climb easily to a level shoulder on the southeast ridge near 7,200 ft. From there make a rising traverse on scree westward beneath the face to the snow patches under its lower cliff band, often moving in the shallow moat where the snow has pulled away from the rock. Those snowfields are steep enough to want crampons late in the season, and the break in the cliff band above them stays hidden until you are almost underneath it.

waypoints.name: Jack Mountain summit
waypoints.note: True summit gained via a notch just west of the summit blocks followed by a short, exposed class-3 finish.
waypoints.directions: Above the cliff band the face gives 400-500 ft of class 3 ramps and ledges strung together by harder class 4 steps and traverses, then eases into straightforward scrambling and a band of scree beside a snow patch that returns you to the southeast ridge near 8,600 ft. Traverse and drop slightly to get in under the summit cliffs, then take the partly snow-filled gully above at class 3 and 4 with one step that can feel low fifth. Holds pull off freely on all of it, so keep the party spread sideways rather than stacked in the gully.

waypoints.name: Pete Lake Trailhead
waypoints.note: Self-issue wilderness permit at the kiosk plus a Northwest Forest Pass or $5 day-use fee for parking; reached via I-90 exit 80, SR-903, FR-46, FR-4616.
waypoints.directions: From I-90 Exit 80 at Roslyn/Salmon la Sac, drive north on SR-903 for 16.8 miles through Roslyn and past Cle Elum Lake, then west on Forest Road 46 for 4.7 miles, and turn right on FR-4616 for one mile to the Cooper Lake/Pete Lake trailhead. Self-issue a wilderness permit at the trailhead kiosk, and bring a Northwest Forest Pass or pay the $5 day-use fee for parking.

waypoints.name: Pete Lake
waypoints.note: Established lakeside campsites and the last easy, reliable water before climbing toward the PCT and Lemah basin.

waypoints.name: Lemah Creek ford at PCT junction
waypoints.note: The old footbridge is washed out; ford cold, sometimes shin-to-thigh-deep Lemah Creek where the Pete Lake trail meets the PCT.

waypoints.name: Lemah Meadows basin camp
waypoints.note: Climbers' bivy sites in the boggy meadow below Lemah's east face, reached via an overgrown climbers' path north of the creek; last reliable water before the basin.

waypoints.name: Basin between Lemah One and Lemah Two
waypoints.note: Gain the crest here and contour north around Lemah Two's east buttress toward the base of the summit cliff bands, per route beta.

waypoints.name: Class 3-4 cliff band / chute below the col
waypoints.note: Crux of the climb: loose rock and often lingering steep snow/ice in the chute leading up toward the col between Lemah Two and Lemah Main.

waypoints.name: Lemah Two
waypoints.note: Highest of the two southern false summits on the Lemah massif ridge; short exposed ledges lead to the top. [Coordinate corrected 2026-08-19: the stored pin held the Pete Lake Trailhead's position (56 m from it, 4,480 ft below this summit). Replaced with the peak's own coordinate, which the route's 221-point track passes within 3 m of.]

waypoints.name: Goodell Creek Trailhead
waypoints.note: Standard, single approach for all Southern Pickets/Terror Basin objectives including Little Mac Spire.

waypoints.name: Goodell Creek Crossings
waypoints.note: Trail fords two branches of Goodell Creek that run high on hot afternoons; a small streamside campsite sits near the second crossing.

waypoints.name: Terror Creek Cairn / Climbers' Path
waypoints.note: Large cairn and stone arrow mark the turn off the maintained Goodell Creek trail onto the steep, faint climbers' path south of Terror Creek — the start of the '~4,000 ft over 2 mi' push.

waypoints.name: Rocky Streambed Source
waypoints.note: Last dependable water on the climbers' path, running in a rocky streambed; the faint tread resumes just upstream.

waypoints.name: Terror Basin Notch
waypoints.note: Gap on the east rim of Terror Basin reached via a rising traverse over moderate snow into midsummer; first view down onto the basin and the McMillan/Little Mac group.

waypoints.name: Terror Basin Camp
waypoints.note: Shared high camp for the whole McMillan/Terror cluster — flat gravel benches, running water, and rock-walled bivy sites; base for Little Mac, East Mac, and West Mac.

waypoints.name: Loose Rock Below the Summit Block
waypoints.note: Southern Pickets rock is notoriously fractured here; test holds and stagger climbers on the short 5.4 pitch to avoid knocking rock onto partners below.

waypoints.name: Little Mac Spire
waypoints.note: Approximate — no independently surveyed summit coordinate found for this minor Southern Pickets spire; cross-referenced against neighboring McMillan/Terror group summits and the route's recorded approach track to place it as close to the true high point as available sources allow.

waypoints.name: Elbow Lake Trailhead (FR 38, north access)
waypoints.note: North trailhead for Elbow Lake Trail 697, ~11 mi up FR 38 from Mosquito Lake Rd; FR 38 is gated Dec 1–Jun 15 at Wallace Creek and there's no bridge over the Middle Fork Nooksack from here.
waypoints.directions: Reach the trailhead by way of Mosquito Lake Road and Forest Road 38, on the north side of the Twin Sisters range. FR 38 runs roughly 11 miles of gravel from the Mosquito Lake Road junction to the trailhead. The road is gated at Wallace Creek from December 1 through June 15 for elk winter range, so this approach only works as a summer and fall objective.

waypoints.name: Middle Fork Nooksack River ford
waypoints.note: Unofficial log/boulder crossing (sometimes a placed logjam) just downstream of the trailhead; can be unfordable at high flow, check recent conditions before committing.

waypoints.name: Green Creek Climbers' Trail split
waypoints.note: Flagged climbers' path branches off the Elbow Lake Trail near Hildebrand Creek and drops into the Green Creek drainage; easy to miss, watch for blue trail markers.

waypoints.name: "The Spa" bivy basin
waypoints.note: Sandy bivy pockets among big boulders (some overhead-sheltered) with two reliable fresh-water springs; the standard base camp for Green Creek Cirque objectives.

waypoints.name: Green Creek Arete base (5.6 crux)
waypoints.note: Foot of the roughly 2-hour-from-trailhead arete that stairsteps up to the upper cirque; mostly solid 3rd/4th class olivine broken by one distinct 5.6 move.

waypoints.name: Green Creek (Sisters) Glacier crossing
waypoints.note: Glacial slabs above the arete lead onto the Green Creek/Sisters Glacier; crevasses and perched snow open up by late summer — rope up if snow-covered.

waypoints.name: Little Sister NW Face base
waypoints.note: About 100 ft of sustained 5.4 face climbing on the NW aretes before the angle eases into 3rd/4th class scrambling to the top; exposed, and route-finding gets tricky if clouds move in.

waypoints.name: Little Sister
waypoints.note: True summit above the Green Creek Cirque; most parties descend by reversing the NW Face or dropping the SE Ridge back toward the glacier.

waypoints.name: Ross Dam / Big Beaver Trailhead (Hwy 20)
waypoints.note: Car trailhead on Hwy 20 (Big Beaver Trail start); approach to Luna Cirque/Phantom Peak via Ross Lake, Big Beaver Trail, Access Creek, Luna Pass.

waypoints.name: Phantom Peak summit
waypoints.note: Phantom Peak's own summit, elev 8016 ft. Luna Glacier is an approach to Phantom Peak itself, not to Luna Peak — a different, nearby peak.

waypoints.name: Goodell Creek / Upper Goodell Group Camp trailhead (SR-20, Newhalem)
waypoints.note: Old overgrown roadbed departs SR 20 here paralleling Goodell Creek; NOCA backcountry permit (from the Marblemount Wilderness Info Center) required for any overnight.
waypoints.directions: From SR-20 near Newhalem, turn off just east of Goodell Creek Campground to reach the Goodell Creek Upper Group Campground trailhead, at about 600 feet, where the old overgrown roadbed departs the highway paralleling Goodell Creek. The unsigned climbers' path itself starts behind a large boulder near the campground. A North Cascades National Park backcountry permit, available from the Marblemount Wilderness Info Center, is required for any overnight.

waypoints.name: Stone-arrow/cairn turnoff to Terror Basin path
waypoints.note: A stone arrow/large cairn at the end of the old Goodell Creek roadbed marks the unsigned turnoff onto the boot path climbing toward Terror Basin; easy to walk past.
waypoints.directions: Pick the path up on the east side of Goodell Creek — it starts behind a large boulder near the campground, not at the campground sign on the west bank — then follow the old roadbed up the valley at a gentle grade. It is unmaintained: dozens of downed logs and a couple of washouts make these four miles far slower than the profile suggests, so budget two to four hours rather than judging pace by the mileage.

waypoints.name: Last water before the hill climb
waypoints.note: No reliable water again until Terror Basin, so tank up here before the steep 4,000 ft climb begins.
waypoints.directions: The boot path leaves the end of the roadbed and enters the trees, gaining only a hundred feet or so before reaching this crossing. It is a few minutes' walk, and the last flat ground before the climbing starts in earnest.

waypoints.name: Treeline / heather benches
waypoints.note: Boot-beaten path gains roughly 4,000 ft in 2 miles (steeper than the old Mailbox Peak trail) before breaking out of forest onto open heather and rock benches.
waypoints.directions: From here the path turns straight uphill and gains roughly 4,000 ft in about two miles on a steep, unrelenting boot track with more blowdown to duck. Near 4,000 ft it crosses a small talus field, swings left, and makes a rising traverse beneath a rock band around 4,800 ft before kicking up one last steep gully onto open ground.

waypoints.name: Terror Basin camp
waypoints.note: Gravelly wildflower basin with several small streams; the established tent sites here are the standard base camp, roughly 3:15 in from the trailhead.
waypoints.directions: Heather benches and granite slabs lead north for a couple of miles to a notch in the ridge crest at roughly 6,200-6,350 ft, the high point of the whole approach. The north side of that notch is the crux of getting in, not the climb: about 400 vertical feet of steep, loose choss when it is melted out — stay skier's-right, as going straight down is a bad idea — or a firmer snow finger when it is filled in, capped by a short steep headwall that some parties rope up for or protect with a lower.

waypoints.name: The Barrier traverse
waypoints.note: Serious class-3 crossing of the ridge separating Terror Creek and Crescent Creek basins via a steep, loose grassy ledge (~6,100 ft) up to the crest (~6,400 ft); heavily exposed, loose rock, described by climbers as a 'slip-and-die' section.

waypoints.name: Crescent Creek basin / 7,200 ft col
waypoints.note: After descending into Crescent Creek basin, heather/snow/rock leads back up to this col on the west ridge — the same col used again on the downclimb.
waypoints.directions: From the crest of the Barrier, descend into the Crescent Creek basin, then climb back up heather, snow and rock to the col on the west ridge — the same col you will use again on the downclimb.

waypoints.name: West McMillan Spire summit
waypoints.note: True summit of West McMillan Spire (Grade III, 5.6 on the west ridge); Southern Pickets high point with exposed final scrambling/low 5th class moves.
waypoints.directions: Above the col the ridge relaxes into a long scramble on scree, heather and broken rock, with a choice between more solid rock steps and looser talus. There is no sustained difficulty, but the footing is poor enough to make it slow in both directions, and rockfall onto a party strung out below is the main hazard here — keep the group tight. A short, exposed step gains the summit block: it starts loose and scree-covered before the rock improves markedly near the top, and the exposure concentrates in the last few moves between the false summit and the true one, where the crest narrows and drops away on both sides. Some parties fix a hand line for that stretch.

waypoints.name: Monument (Lost River) Trailhead
waypoints.note: Free self-issue wilderness permit required at trailhead kiosk; FR-5400 gravel spur reached via Lost River Road out of Mazama.
waypoints.directions: Drive Lost River Road out of Mazama, about 22 miles northwest of Winthrop, onto the FR-5400 gravel spur to the trailhead. Fill out the free self-issue wilderness permit at the kiosk.

waypoints.name: Eureka Creek Ford
waypoints.note: Bridge here washed out in 2006 and was never replaced; ford can be a tricky, thigh-deep crossing in early-season high water, last reliable water before the long dry climb to Pistol Ridge.
waypoints.directions: Follow Monument Creek Trail No. 484 up the Lost River valley. The first 4 miles are well maintained, running through old-growth forest and along rock slopes to the confluence and Eureka Falls Camp. The bridge here washed out in 2006 and was never replaced, so the crossing is a ford; it can run thigh-deep and cold during snowmelt. This is the last easy, reliable water before a long dry climb.

waypoints.name: Pistol Pass
waypoints.note: Abandoned, brushy tread climbs ~4,700 ft from the ford onto Pistol Ridge before improving near the pass; from here the maintained trail effectively ends and route-finding begins.
waypoints.directions: Beyond the ford the trail has been essentially unmaintained for over 25 years, brushy and choked with deadfall, and route-finding becomes real work. Pick up the abandoned tread climbing onto Pistol Ridge and follow it for about 4,700 ft of gain; the tread improves near the top. Expect 4 to 5 hours from the creek and plan on running out of water.

waypoints.name: Lake of the Woods
waypoints.note: Small alpine lake about a mile below Pistol Pass with established campsites; the standard staging camp for the Monument Peak / Lake Mountain 'Monumental Slam.'
waypoints.directions: From the pass, side-hill cross-country down into the Monument and Lake Mountain basin to the small alpine lake, roughly a mile below the pass. Established campsites here make the standard staging camp for the peak.

waypoints.name: Lake Mountain South Ridge Saddle
waypoints.note: Cross-country gain from Lake of the Woods over Lake Mountain's south ridge saddle, the start of the side-hill traverse toward Monument Peak.
waypoints.directions: Traverse cross-country from the lake, gaining ground over Lake Mountain's south ridge saddle. Reckon on about 2 hours from camp; this is where the side-hill traverse toward Monument Peak begins.

waypoints.name: Lower Monument Basin
waypoints.note: Descend off the saddle into this basin below Monument's south side; used as a bivy/staging spot by parties splitting the peak from Lake Mountain.
waypoints.directions: Drop off the saddle into the basin below Monument's south side, losing about 1,300 ft. The lake-outlet creek here is the last dependable water for the summit push and can be down to a trickle late in the season, so fill up.

waypoints.name: South Ridge Crest (Ramp System)
waypoints.note: Left-angling ramp system out of Lower Monument Basin gains the crest of the south ridge; this is the ramp used by the descent.
waypoints.directions: From the basin, climb the left-angling ramp system that gains the crest of the south ridge, about 800 ft of ascent. This is the ramp the descent beta also refers to, so note where you topped out.

waypoints.name: Monument Peak Summit
waypoints.note: Long talus traverse along the south ridge ends at the 'leaning summit horn,' with Class 3 scrambling on the final blocks (first ascent Beckey/Roper, 1978).
waypoints.directions: Follow the broad ridge for over a mile of class 2 talus walking toward the summit, with light class 3 in spots.
