A short class 3 scramble surmounts the false summit near 8,000 ft, then one or two more class 3 moves on the steep upper mountain reach the leaning summit horn. A steep snowfield just below the top sometimes lingers into midsummer and either needs an axe or a class 3-4 rock detour around its left side. Roughly 3 hours from the ridge crest.

waypoints.name: Easy Pass Trailhead
waypoints.note: Signed pullout on SR-20 near milepost 151-152 (45 mi east of Marblemount); Northwest Forest Pass required, self-issue NPS wilderness permit if bivying beyond the pass.

waypoints.name: Easy Pass Creek footlog crossing
waypoints.note: Trail crosses Easy Pass Creek (feeds Granite Creek) on a log; it gets sketchy/submerged in high snowmelt water.

waypoints.name: Easy Pass
waypoints.note: Trail high point and North Cascades NP boundary; leave the maintained tread here and drop west off-trail toward Fisher Creek to reach Arriva's basin.

waypoints.name: Fisher Creek Basin (below Arriva)
waypoints.note: Off-trail boot/talus descent from the pass lands in the open basin under Arriva's south/southwest aspect; the maintained Fisher Creek Trail continues down-valley to Fisher Camp (~2 mi further) if splitting the approach over two days.

waypoints.name: Talus and snow apron below the SW slopes
waypoints.note: Loose talus interspersed with lingering snowfields/moats guards the base of the climbing line; carry an ice axe into midsummer and watch for hidden meltwater gaps under the snow edge.

waypoints.name: Notch gaining the south/southwest ridge
waypoints.note: Rising traverse across a talus bowl reaches this notch, the gateway into the short Class 3 rock bands and ledge systems leading to the summit block.

waypoints.name: Mount Arriva summit
waypoints.note: True (West) summit of Mount Arriva, first climbed 1966; despite sitting only 1.5 mi from Easy Pass it is hidden from the pass and the highway, so route-finding on the final rock bands is the crux.

waypoints.name: Mill Creek ford
waypoints.note: Ford Mill Creek just below the trail junction — last reliable, easy-to-reach water before the long climb toward Azurite.

waypoints.name: Mill Creek Trail junction
waypoints.note: Leave the Canyon Creek tread here and turn up the Mill Creek/Azurite Pass Trail; maintained trail effectively ends beyond this point.

waypoints.name: Overgrown Mill Creek Trail
waypoints.note: Tread disappears under heavy slide alder and downed timber left from the mine-era trail's disuse — expect a slow, scratchy alder-hacking bushwhack for several miles.

waypoints.name: Azurite Mine
waypoints.note: Flat ground amid the old defunct copper/silver mine workings on Mill Creek; the common overnight camp before pushing toward the Ballard basin.

waypoints.name: Azurite–Ballard basin
waypoints.note: Reached via roughly 3 more brush-choked miles above the mine; open basin at the base of Ballard's south slopes and a typical bivy before the summit push.

waypoints.name: South-face brush and gully route-finding
waypoints.note: Steep, loose terrain with several look-alike chutes low on the south face — picking the wrong gully here is the main way parties get cliffed out or turned back.

waypoints.name: Canyon Creek Trailhead
waypoints.note: Standard access: park at Harts Pass (gate/end of maintained Harts Pass Rd), descend Slate Creek Road ~5+ mi west to South Fork Slate Creek bridge, then bushwhack/scramble up the east ridge to the summit. Note that the 'Canyon Creek Trailhead' ~10 mi away on Hwy 20 is a real but unrelated trailhead that does not access Mount Ballard.

waypoints.name: Sol Duc Trailhead (end of Sol Duc Hot Springs Road)
waypoints.note: Sol Duc trailhead at the end of Sol Duc Hot Springs Road, the start of the High Divide / Bailey Range approach. This REPLACES a pin naming Whiskey Bend, 11.7 mi away on the Elwha, which approaches Mount Barnes from the opposite end and never passes Heart Lake — the first waypoint here. Every recorded distance on this route is consistent with a Sol Duc start. Coordinate from published sources rather than the Park Service, which does not publish one.

waypoints.name: Heart Lake
waypoints.note: Last reliable water and common camp before crossing High Divide; there is no water again until well past the Catwalk toward Eleven Bull Basin.

waypoints.name: High Divide crest near Bogachiel Peak
waypoints.note: Maintained High Divide Trail tops out here; this is where the Bailey Range Traverse leaves the trail and drops off-trail east into Cat Basin toward Cat Peak. The exact off-trail departure point is not recorded separately, so this marker sits on the peak itself.

waypoints.name: The Catwalk (Cat Peak-Mt. Carrie arete)
waypoints.note: Narrow, exposed ridgeline with a few scrambling moves and roughly 3,000 ft of air to the valley floor; poorly defined in fog, not a place to be in wind or wet rock.

waypoints.name: Upper Ferry Basin / Ferry Glacial Lake
waypoints.note: Open meadow below Mount Ferry with glacial lakes and streams for the last dependable water before the Bear Pass approach; established informal camp used by most Bailey Range parties.

waypoints.name: Childs Glacier crossing
waypoints.note: Small glacier/permanent snowfield below Bear Pass; parties report needing ice axe and microspikes on firm snow, with crevasse-type terrain in Junkyard Basin just beyond.

waypoints.name: Bear Pass
waypoints.note: Broad saddle marking the southeastern terminus of the Bailey Range proper; from here the route drops toward a flat meadow before angling southeast for the final Barnes approach.

waypoints.name: Sol Duc Trailhead
waypoints.note: Large trailhead parking lot at the end of Sol Duc Hot Springs Road; Northwest Forest Pass required, self-issue wilderness permit at the kiosk.
waypoints.directions: Turn south off US 101 onto Sol Duc Hot Springs Road (about 29 miles west of Port Angeles) and follow it, paved the whole way, past the park entrance station, the Sol Duc Hot Springs Resort and the campground to the large lot at road's end — the trailhead is at the very end, beyond the resort.

waypoints.name: Sol Duc Falls
waypoints.note: Trail crosses a footbridge just below the falls; last easy, reliable water before the climb toward Appleton Pass begins in earnest.
waypoints.directions: From the end of the lot take the Sol Duc River Trail up the valley: 0.8 mi of wide, near-level old-growth tread with essentially no elevation change (1,950 to 1,980 ft), ending at the footbridge just below the falls. This is the last easy, reliable water taken straight off the trail before the climbing starts.

waypoints.name: Appleton Pass Trail junction
waypoints.note: Leave the Sol Duc River Trail here and turn right/uphill onto the Appleton Pass Trail; elevation is a rough interpolation along the NPS-stated 2,000-5,100 ft climb.

waypoints.name: Appleton Pass
waypoints.note: Broad alpine pass on the Bailey Range crest with meadows and views into the Boulder Lake basin; leave the maintained trail here to begin cross-country travel into the Bailey Range proper.

waypoints.name: The Cat Walk (Cat Peak traverse)
waypoints.note: Old, narrow, exposed use-path sidehilling the steep flanks of Cat Peak; the steepest, most exposure-prone stretch of the whole approach, worse with a full pack.

waypoints.name: Boston Charlie's Camp
waypoints.note: Small flat tent spot at the east end of the Cat Walk with a shallow melt-water sinkhole pond; water needs filtering and the site is exposed to wind/weather.
waypoints.directions: Follow the sidehill path east to the far end of the Cat Walk arete, giving back roughly 200 ft. The camp is a single small flat tent spot at the east end with a shallow melt-water sinkhole pond beside it — filter that water, and expect the site to be fully exposed to wind and weather.

waypoints.name: Mount Carrie ridge/glacier gain
waypoints.note: Highest point in the Bailey Range (0.84 mi SW of Fairchild's summit); per the descent beta this is where the route regains the ridge/glacier system linking to the Fairchild Glacier.
waypoints.directions: Climb roughly 1,700 ft southeast from Boston Charlie's onto Mount Carrie (6,995 ft), the highest point in the Bailey Range. There is a real choice here: many parties sidehill the loose, exposed talus across Carrie's south face, but staying higher — up the ridge on Carrie's north side, over or just under the summit — avoids the worst of the sidehilling and sets up a cleaner entry onto the Fairchild Glacier. Where the crest becomes too sharp to walk, traverse up across the scree flanks. There is no reliable water on this stretch, so tank up at camp.

waypoints.name: Fairchild Glacier crossing
waypoints.note: Rope up and don crampons/axe here; follow the wind-formed ridge down-glacier toward the exit col on Ruth Peak's shoulder — crevasse hazard, especially late season when snow bridges are thin.
waypoints.directions: Drop about 300 ft northeast off Carrie's ridge onto the upper Fairchild Glacier, which starts around 6,600-6,700 ft on the Bailey crest and falls away to the northeast. Rope up and put on crampons here; an ice axe is wanted most of the season. Rather than taking the direct line, follow the wind-formed snow ridge running down the glacier — the same idea as the Hogsback on Mount Hood — which keeps you clear of the crevasses. Late season the snow bridges thin and the surface goes to bare, hard ice, so this is full crampon technique, not microspikes.

waypoints.name: Mount Fairchild
waypoints.note: Second-highest peak in the Bailey Range; short final scramble on snow and rock from the glacier saddle to the true summit.
waypoints.directions: Leave the wind ridge and take the steeper exit section up onto Fairchild's summit ridge: roughly 35-40 degrees of snow past an icy patch, the steepest ground on the route. Stay roped and in crampons through it. From the summit ridge a short scramble on snow and rock gains the 6,899 ft true summit, second-highest in the Bailey Range. There is no rappel anywhere on this climb — the only way off is to reverse the entire line, and the glacier softens through the afternoon, so set an early turnaround.

waypoints.name: Sol Duc Trailhead (Olympic NP)
waypoints.note: Northwest Forest Pass required for parking; wilderness permits (recreation.gov) needed for overnight camps on the Sol Duc/High Divide corridor.

waypoints.name: Sol Duc Falls
waypoints.note: Boardwalk viewpoint over the falls and junction with the Lover's Lane Trail; stay on the Deer Lake/High Divide Trail.

waypoints.name: Deer Lake
waypoints.note: Established backcountry camp with bear wires; last easy water and flat tent sites before the steep climb to High Divide.

waypoints.name: Heart Lake
waypoints.note: Last reliable water before the dry, exposed Cat Peak-Mt. Carrie ridge section - top off here.

waypoints.name: High Divide - Cat Basin Trail Junction
waypoints.note: Maintained trail ends near here; the unmarked Bailey Range 'primitive route' splits off High Divide toward Cat Peak and off-trail routefinding begins.

waypoints.name: The Catwalk (Cat Peak-Mt. Carrie arete)
waypoints.note: Narrow, exposed ridge traverse on loose rock linking Cat Peak and Mount Carrie; a slip on the steep side-hill sections could mean a long uncontrolled fall.

waypoints.name: Ferry Basin
waypoints.note: Open meadow basin below Mount Ferry's south slopes with glacial tarns for camping/swimming, reached via a col just south of Stephen Peak (~5,900 ft).

waypoints.name: Mount Ferry
waypoints.note: Class 2-3 scramble off the main Bailey Range traverse near the Ferry-Pulitzer col; broad summit with views across Queets Basin to Mount Olympus.

waypoints.name: Bagley Lakes Trailhead / Heather Meadows
waypoints.note: South end of the upper Mt. Baker Ski Area parking lot off SR 542; Northwest Forest Pass required to park, self-issue fee machine at the lot.

waypoints.name: Bagley Lakes
waypoints.note: Trail skirts the Bagley Lakes basin shortly after the trailhead; last easy, reliable water before the climb toward Herman Saddle.

waypoints.name: Chain Lakes Trail — leave-trail point for the Herman gully
waypoints.note: Chain Lakes Trail is followed to about 4,500 ft, where climbers peel off trail and start up the gully toward Herman Saddle; no cairns, easy to miss in cloud.

waypoints.name: Herman Saddle
waypoints.note: Broad saddle between Mazama Dome and Mount Herman with views of Baker, Shuksan and Iceberg Lake below; the true col is variously placed anywhere from ~5,300 to ~5,450 ft.

waypoints.name: Heather-and-talus south slope
waypoints.note: Above the saddle you leave any trail and work up loose heather benches and talus on Herman's broad south face — footing is unstable, especially wet or on the descent.

waypoints.name: Unnamed lake / gully to summit ridge
waypoints.note: A small unnamed tarn sits below a series of cirques; a gully rising directly from it leads to the low point on the summit ridge (near-true scramble, easy 3rd class).

waypoints.name: Mount Herman
waypoints.note: Short east ridge gains the summit block from the ridge low point; descend the same south/southwest ridge and heather-scree gully rather than the east side.

waypoints.name: Necklace Valley Trailhead
waypoints.note: End of FR 68, 4.1 mi from US Hwy 2 at Skykomish; self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit and Northwest Forest Pass required at the kiosk.
waypoints.directions: The trailhead sits at the end of Forest Road 68, about 4.1 miles from US Highway 2 at Skykomish, at roughly 1,650 feet. A self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit and a Northwest Forest Pass are required at the trailhead kiosk.

waypoints.name: East Fork Foss River crossing
waypoints.note: Log or ford crossing of the East Fork Foss near an established camp; the first 5 miles gain only ~600 ft but this crossing can be tricky during high runoff.

waypoints.name: Jade Lake
waypoints.note: First of the Necklace Valley lakes and the common base camp for Hinman climbs; trail steepens sharply above the river crossing, gaining roughly 2,400 ft in about 3 miles to reach it.

waypoints.name: La Bohn Gap
waypoints.note: Cairned climbers' path through boulder fields and heather gains this notch on the ridge crest above La Bohn Lakes; avoid the waterfall drainage to the left, routefinding is poor in fog.

waypoints.name: Hinman/Foss Glacier remnant snowfield
waypoints.note: Traverse of the shrinking glacier remnant below the west ridge; carry ice axe and crampons/microspikes for firm morning snow, and watch for isolated moats or crevasses late season.

waypoints.name: Mount Hinman summit
waypoints.note: Broad, multi-humped summit ridge where the true high point is ambiguous; final approach involves a short loose 4th-class scramble near the east end.

waypoints.name: Jefferson Creek Crossing (FR 2401)
waypoints.note: Faint climbers' path begins on the north side of the creek where FSR 2401 fords Jefferson Creek; park in the turnout just after the crossing (Northwest Forest Pass area, no formal trailhead sign).
waypoints.directions: From Hoodsport, drive about 14 miles north on US 101 to the Hamma Hamma River Road (FR 25) and follow it roughly 6.5 miles to FR 2480. Take FR 2480 about 3 miles to FR 2401, then FR 2401 another 7 to 7.5 miles to where it crosses Jefferson Creek, in the Jefferson Lake trailhead area at about 2,440 feet. Park in the turnout just after the crossing — there is no formal trailhead sign, and it is a Northwest Forest Pass area. Confirm current road status with Olympic National Forest before you drive: FR 2480 and FR 2401 have a history of washouts and were briefly closed during the 2025 Hamma Fire, though that closure has since been rescinded.

waypoints.name: Jefferson Creek (last reliable water)
waypoints.note: Path follows the north bank through old-growth forest, boulders, and windfall — fill up here, as the route goes dry once it climbs into the gully and basins above.

waypoints.name: Rocky gully to 4,300' basin
waypoints.note: After several hundred feet of forest/brush the path makes a rising traverse into a rocky gully; climb the gully to a small basin at roughly 4,300 ft — this is also the point to aim for on the descent before dropping back to the creek.

waypoints.name: Upper basin (cut left below summit)
waypoints.note: From the 4,300' basin continue straight up then cut left up a second gully into the basin east of the summit at about 5,400 ft, staged at the base of the final snow/rock gully.

waypoints.name: Snow gully + Class 4 rock step
waypoints.note: 45–50 degree snow leads to a short pitch of loose, brushy Class 4 rock gaining the summit ridge; carry an ice axe/crampons — this step has caught unprepared parties.

waypoints.name: Knife-edge ridge traverse
waypoints.note: Ridge crest is mostly Class 2–3 but narrows to a genuinely knife-edge section with one or two exposed Class 3/4 moves just before the summit block.

waypoints.name: Mount Pershing, South Peak
waypoints.note: True (south) summit of the Pershing massif's three tops, 1.3 mi NNW of Mount Washington; allow a full day, historically cited as ~11 hours car-to-car.

waypoints.name: Ross Dam Trailhead
waypoints.note: SR-20 parking near milepost 134; self-issue NPS wilderness permit required well ahead for Big Beaver/Ross Lake camps before starting.

waypoints.name: Big Beaver Trail junction (via Ross Dam)
waypoints.note: Cross Ross Dam and follow the Ross Lake shoreline to the Big Beaver Trail junction; Ross Lake Resort's water taxi to Big Beaver Landing can bypass this shoreline stretch.

waypoints.name: Thirtynine Mile Creek Camp
waypoints.note: Tent sites on the west bank, stock/horse camp on the east bank of Thirtynine Mile Creek; the last reliable running water and last legal campsite before leaving the trail.

waypoints.name: Off-trail departure onto Thirtynine Mile Ridge
waypoints.note: Leave Big Beaver Trail between the creek crossing and the 'Thirtynine Mile Creek Camp' marker post, climbing north through a brushy gully and adjacent rib — reported as a horrible bushwhack low down.

waypoints.name: Point 6071, Thirtynine Mile Ridge crest
waypoints.note: Ridge crest gained here; travel eases to open Class 1-2 walking above this point after steep timber and brush below.

waypoints.name: Saddle camp below Point 6690, South Ridge
waypoints.note: Informal saddle campsite used to split the climb into two days; no running water — carry up from Thirtynine Mile Creek.

waypoints.name: Points 7361 and 7547 (false summits)
waypoints.note: Exposed rocky high points along the crest before the true summit; the descent requires down-climbing short Class 3 steps here in reverse.

waypoints.name: Mount Prophet summit
waypoints.note: True summit reached via a short Class 3 rock scramble on the final southeast ridge; exposure is present but never bad.

waypoints.name: North Fork Quinault / Irely Lake Trailhead
waypoints.note: Road's end on North Shore Road above Lake Quinault; Wilderness Information Center permit required, start of the Three Lakes / Skyline Ridge Primitive Trail.

waypoints.name: Three Lakes
waypoints.note: Established camp beside the largest of the Three Lakes (moss-covered shoreline); water from the outlet stream just north of the sites is the last dependable source before a dry 5.2-mile stretch toward Kimta Peak.

waypoints.name: Kimta Peak
waypoints.note: Skyline Ridge Primitive Trail sidehills Kimta Peak's south flank; parties camp on a gravel flat in Kimta Basin here after the waterless stretch from Three Lakes.

waypoints.name: Promise Creek Bench
waypoints.note: High point of the Skyline Trail; NPS describes 'lunar-esque' loose rocky terrain here that demands careful routefinding, especially in fog.

waypoints.name: Beauty (Lake Beauty) Pass
waypoints.note: Ridge crossing marked by cairns and marker ducks; a 0.3-mile spur drops to Lake Beauty camp with a view of Mount Olympus's south face.

waypoints.name: Low Divide
waypoints.note: Saddle between Mount Seattle and Mount Christie and the terminus of the Skyline Ridge Primitive Trail, near the historic Low Divide Ranger Station site.

waypoints.name: Seattle Meadows
waypoints.note: High camp in Upper Seattle Basin reached via a ~1,000 ft climb from Seattle Creek; standard launch point for the summit scramble, per route beta.

waypoints.name: Mount Seattle
waypoints.note: True summit gained by a Class 2-3 scramble up the east ridge, crossing scree and talus slopes on the peak's eastern side above Upper Seattle Basin.

waypoints.name: Nooksack Cirque Trailhead
waypoints.note: End of FR 34 (via Mt Baker Hwy SR 542, Hannegan Pass Rd FR 32, then FR 34); ford Ruth Creek immediately at the trailhead — no bridge, wade it or cross a downed log if present.
waypoints.directions: From Glacier, drive Mt. Baker Highway (SR-542) east about 12.5 miles, then turn left onto Hannegan Pass Road (FR-32). Continue just over a mile to the junction with Nooksack Cirque Road (FR-34) and follow FR-34 one mile to its end at the Nooksack Cirque Trailhead, which is a different trailhead from the Hannegan Pass Trailhead further up FR-32. Ford Ruth Creek right at the trailhead — there's no bridge, so wade it or cross a downed log if one is present, and note that early-summer high water can make the crossing difficult or unsafe.

waypoints.name: Leave Trail #750 roadbed
waypoints.note: About 50 minutes up the old logging roadbed (Trail #750), leave the trail and begin an ascending traverse up through forest toward Sefrit's west/southwest ridge — no path, route-finding required.

waypoints.name: Brushy ascending traverse
waypoints.note: Steep forest with slide alder and old avalanche debris on the traverse toward the ridge crest — slick brush and rotten downed timber slow travel on this south-facing approach.

waypoints.name: 5800' meadows on ridge crest
waypoints.note: Brush opens into subalpine meadows around 5800 ft on the ridge, giving easy open travel across to the summit gully — the same feature crossed by the parallel south-side route off this trailhead.

waypoints.name: Class 4 summit gully
waypoints.note: Loose, blocky Class 4 gully breaches the final rock band to the summit ridge; this is the gully down-climbed on the reverse descent.

waypoints.name: Mount Sefrit summit
waypoints.note: Broad rocky summit block 4 miles north of Mount Shuksan, overlooking the Nooksack Cirque and North Fork Nooksack headwaters.

waypoints.name: Huckleberry Creek crossing
waypoints.note: Trail drops into a brushy ravine to ford Huckleberry Creek — last reliable water before the root-ladder climb, and easy to lose in poor light.

waypoints.name: Root-ladder ridge highpoint (4,100 ft)
waypoints.note: Crux of the approach: gains roughly 1,000 ft in about a half mile on hand-and-foot root and rock ladders (one pitch near 75-80 degrees) to the trail's high ridge crest.

waypoints.name: Mildred Lakes basin (Lower/Upper Mildred Lake)
waypoints.note: Trail drops ~250 ft off the ridge to Lower Mildred Lake then continues past Middle to Upper Mildred Lake in a wooded bowl between Mount Lincoln and Mount Cruiser; informal camps on rock benches, last dependable water before going off-trail.

waypoints.name: Off-trail brush slope above the lakes
waypoints.note: Route leaves the lakeshore path entirely here; slide-alder and heather bushwhacking, very brushy as on neighboring Mt. Cruiser, and much easier with lingering snow cover.

waypoints.name: Basin/saddle below Skokomish's south peak
waypoints.note: Gain the open basin and connecting saddle beneath the summit block; footing turns to loose, notoriously rotten rock from here up.

waypoints.name: Duckabush Trailhead
waypoints.note: Road-end trailhead on Duckabush Trail #803 (FR 2510-060); self-issue day pass/NW Forest Pass at the kiosk, plus an Olympic NP wilderness permit once you cross the park boundary.

waypoints.name: Ten-Mile Camp
waypoints.note: Established Duckabush River camp with a privy and bear wires; last easy, reliable water and legal campsite before the climb into subalpine terrain.

waypoints.name: Duckabush Camp creek turnoff
waypoints.note: Leave the maintained Duckabush Trail here, about 3 mi below Marmot Lake, and follow the unmarked feeder creek toward the amphitheater below Steel's west face.

waypoints.name: Steep push below Marmot Lake
waypoints.note: The final mile up to Marmot Lake gains elevation fast on loose, eroded tread; it is the most exhausting stretch of the approach.

waypoints.name: Marmot Lake
waypoints.note: Standard backcountry basecamp for this route, 1.2 mi below O'Neil Pass, with views across the basin to Mts. Duckabush and Steel.

waypoints.name: Amphitheater below west face
waypoints.note: From camp, drop back roughly 3 mi to the creek junction and climb into this open basin; easy slopes lead to the summit from here but can hold snow into July, requiring an ice axe.

waypoints.name: Mount Steel Summit
waypoints.note: True summit (Class 2-3); the peak rises over 3,400 ft above the Duckabush River in roughly one mile, giving abrupt views into the LaCrosse Basin and toward Mt. Duckabush.

waypoints.name: Mount Washington Trailhead (FR-2419)
waypoints.note: End of FR-2419 off North Lake Cushman Road/FR 24; self-issue Mt. Skokomish Wilderness permit and Northwest Forest Pass required at the kiosk.
waypoints.directions: From the T-intersection at the end of North Lake Cushman Road, turn right onto FS Road 24 and continue about a mile, then turn left onto FS Road 2419 and follow it up the Big Creek drainage for roughly 6.6 miles to its end at a small trailhead and parking area near 3,026 ft. Fill out a self-issue Mt. Skokomish Wilderness permit and display a Northwest Forest Pass at the kiosk.

waypoints.name: Climbers' path / rock gullies
waypoints.note: Maintained trail gives way to a climbers' path up steep, narrow rock gullies studded with tree roots — hand-over-hand in spots.

waypoints.name: Lower meadow
waypoints.note: Grade eases briefly in an open meadow where the ridgeline and neighboring Mount Ellinor come into view.

waypoints.name: Upper talus/scree field
waypoints.note: Route climbs a broad talus and scree slope above the meadow; footing is loose, watch for rockfall from parties above.

waypoints.name: 5,600' ramp at the headwall
waypoints.note: Crux route-finding point: path swings west onto a ramp that hugs the headwall briefly, then ducks back through trees.

waypoints.name: South saddle
waypoints.note: Known bivy site on the saddle; first spot on the climb where the true summit becomes visible.

waypoints.name: The Catwalk
waypoints.note: Exposed knife-edge ledge crux move on the final ridge; helmet recommended, some parties rig a handline here.

waypoints.name: Mount Washington summit
waypoints.note: True summit (6,255'); exposed east-facing ridge on the final approach, summit register present.

waypoints.name: Slate Pass / Buckskin Ridge Trailhead
waypoints.note: End of Harts Pass Road (FR-5400) near Slate Peak; self-issue Pasayten Wilderness permit at the kiosk, road typically open only July-Sept.
waypoints.directions: Drive Forest Road 5400 from Mazama up to Harts Pass, published at roughly 6,181-6,204 feet - trailers are prohibited past the 5400000/5400060 junction because the road is narrow and steep with few turnouts, and whether an ordinary car should attempt it is genuinely disputed, so judge it on the day. At the guard station turn right onto FR 5400-600; the Pacific Crest Trail trailhead is at the first switchback and Slate Pass, at about 6,900 feet, is at the second. Early in the season you may have to walk the last half mile or so if the road isn't yet clear, and the road itself typically doesn't open until early-to-mid July depending on snowpack. Self-issue a Pasayten Wilderness permit at the kiosk here.

waypoints.name: Middle Fork Pasayten (Robinson Creek) Trail junction
waypoints.note: Reached via Buckskin Ridge Trail (0.9 mi) then Whistler Cutoff Trail (3.1 mi), dropping ~1,900 ft off the pass before turning south down the Middle Fork Pasayten drainage.
waypoints.directions: This leg is all downhill: drop off the pass on the Buckskin Ridge tread, then swing onto the Whistler Cutoff for a well-graded cruise to the valley floor. The first pitch below the pass holds snow well into summer and some parties carry an axe for it. The Middle Fork is crossed unbridged, usually ankle to shin deep in normal summer flow, but it deserves respect during snowmelt or after heavy rain.

waypoints.name: Eureka Creek Trail (#484) junction
waypoints.note: Leave the Middle Fork Pasayten Trail here and start climbing east up Eureka Creek toward Freds Lake; the way tread is brushy and blowdown-choked beyond this point.
waypoints.directions: Turn south and follow the Middle Fork Pasayten trail up the valley. Tread through here is generally good and brush-free, and it is the fastest walking of the trip. Watch for the signed turnoff, which is easy to stride past when the miles are going quickly.

waypoints.name: Freds Lake
waypoints.note: Larch-ringed lake with reliable water and informal camping, the usual overnight stop before pushing on to Freds Pass.
waypoints.directions: Climb east up the Eureka Creek drainage. This is where the trip changes character: tread narrows, brush closes in and stepping over blowdown becomes routine, so expect the pace to drop noticeably. The grade is steady rather than steep, gaining roughly 1,200 ft to the lake basin.

waypoints.name: Freds Pass
waypoints.note: Trail contours Freds Lake's north shore then climbs the head of the basin to this saddle, the gateway into the upper Eureka Creek / Lake Doris basin.
waypoints.directions: Roughly 600 ft of climbing packed into half a mile, which makes this the steepest sustained trail section of the approach. The saddle is open and exposed with no water on it, so top off at the lake before starting up.

waypoints.name: Lake Doris
waypoints.note: Alpine lake basin serving as the standard base camp for Osceola's west slopes; the scramble route starts on the ridge north of the lake.
waypoints.directions: Drop off the far side of the pass and contour down into the next basin, only a couple of hundred feet of loss over about half a mile. Snow can linger on this side early in the season. This is the last water and the standard camp, and everything above it is dry.

waypoints.name: Southwest talus/slab slope
waypoints.note: Loose, sharp talus mixed with slabs that get slick with wet lichen; stay on the faint use-trail through the least-bad line rather than the slabs.
waypoints.directions: From the lake head northeast through open forest and onto the slope above, aiming for the southwest ridge rather than straight up the south-face boulder field. There is a faint use trail on the ridge and it is far better going than the slabs, which turn genuinely slick where lichen is wet. Figure about 800 ft of gain to reach this point.

waypoints.name: Osceola Peak
waypoints.note: True summit (8,587 ft); broad talus top with views to Mount Lago and Carru across upper Eureka Creek.
waypoints.directions: Continue up on big talus broken by short sections of scree, staying on the faint trail wherever it shows rather than drifting onto the slabs. It is Class 2 with occasional Class 3 steps and about another 800 ft of gain to the broad summit. Nothing here needs a rope, and the descent reverses the same line.

waypoints.name: Eagle Creek/Oval Trailhead
waypoints.note: Self-issue Northwest Forest Pass / $5 day-use fee at the kiosk; trail enters Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness a short way in, vault toilet and stock ramp at the lot.
waypoints.directions: Park at the Eagle Creek/Oval trailhead at about 3,000 ft, at the end of FR 4420-080. Reach it on Twisp River Road/FR 44 roughly 12.5 miles west of Twisp, then turn up the West Buttermilk/FR 4420 spur and follow it to the road's end. There is a vault toilet and a stock ramp at the lot; self-issue a Northwest Forest Pass or pay the $5 day-use fee at the kiosk, and the trail enters the Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness a short way in. The access road and the lake basins are typically snow-free from early July into October.

waypoints.name: Eagle Creek / Oval Creek Trail junction
waypoints.note: Ford the side stream here, then turn left off Eagle Creek Trail #410 onto Oval Creek Trail #410A toward the Oval Lakes basin.

waypoints.name: Oval Creek / Oval Lakes Trail junction
waypoints.note: Bear onto Oval Lakes Trail #410B, which climbs past an old moraine below Gray Peak before dropping into the Oval Lakes basin — this section burned in the 2018 Crescent Fire and is dry/dusty with little shade.

waypoints.name: Middle Oval Lake outflow
waypoints.note: Maintained trail ends at the lake outflow; established stock/backpacker camp with fishing (cutthroat) — this is where you leave the trail and start up open heather/talus toward the Sawtooth crest.

waypoints.name: Saddle on Oval Peak's south ridge
waypoints.note: Gain the Sawtooth crest via open heather and talus above the lake's outflow; no maintained tread here, easy to lose the line in fog or low visibility.

waypoints.name: Talus/boulder field on the south ridge crest
waypoints.note: Broad ridge of loose, sometimes slick talus and large boulders — the crux annoyance of the route (twisted-ankle terrain, not technical).

waypoints.name: Oval Peak
waypoints.note: Highest point in the Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness and of the Methow Mountains; small rock glacier on the north slopes, views of Star, Courtney, and Gray Peaks.

waypoints.name: Dingford Creek Trailhead
waypoints.note: Standard access point via FR-56/Middle Fork Snoqualmie River Road; no day-use fee is currently charged at this specific trailhead (per USFS), though a free self-issue wilderness permit is required beyond it for Alpine Lakes Wilderness travel, and the road washout beyond this point means biking or hiking the closed roadbed toward Dutch Miller Gap.
waypoints.directions: FR-56 up the Middle Fork Snoqualmie to the lot is heavily potholed and rutted; parties in low-clearance cars routinely park short and walk the last stretch, which adds to an already long day.

waypoints.name: Overcoat Lake
waypoints.note: Standard high camp for the route, roughly 10 mi in via the Middle Fork Snoqualmie trail/old roadbed then a steep, unmaintained forested slog above a river ford near the old Dutch Miller Gap Trail; seldom-visited alpine lake below the Overcoat Glacier basin.
waypoints.directions: The continuation of the road past the gate is roughly 7-8 miles of old roadbed to Hardscrabble Horse Camp, and most parties bike it rather than walk it. Beyond that the Dutch Miller Gap Trail runs east along the north bank; the tread is reasonable but summer thimbleberry buries the rocks underfoot. Leave the trail about a mile before it swings toward Williams Lake and ford the river: it can run thigh-to-waist deep, and it is colder and higher on the way back than it was in the morning.

waypoints.name: Rock benches above Overcoat Glacier
waypoints.note: Higher alternate camp on open benches used to shorten summit day; this bivy option sits at roughly 6,600 ft.
waypoints.directions: Above the ford the ground climbs steeply through brush into a rocky corridor of waterfalls and steep faces before opening onto snow and benches. Snow lingers here well past midsummer. The awkward part is a sloping rock step partway up, which is markedly harder to downclimb than to climb and is worth noting for the return.

waypoints.name: Notch on Overcoat Peak's north ridge (Overcoat Col)
waypoints.note: Contour east from camp to this notch to gain the upper Overcoat Glacier; a col of the same name and elevation (~6,800 ft) sits beneath Chimney Rock's east face.
waypoints.directions: Only a couple of hundred feet of net gain, but it is a rising traverse over benches and old snow rather than a walk. The glacier starts immediately on the far side, so rope up and fit crampons at the notch rather than after stepping onto it.

waypoints.name: Overcoat Glacier crossing
waypoints.note: Cross the glacier's lower snowfields toward the peak's southeast side; expect deep crevasses and weak, undermined snow bridges on this rapidly retreating glacier.
waypoints.directions: Drop onto the upper glacier from the notch and work toward the peak's southeast side. Most parties time this route for the tail end of summer, when the crevasses are open and visible and the rock above is clear of snow; earlier in the season the bridges are the thing that will catch you out.

waypoints.name: Snow finger to east face
waypoints.note: Find the snow finger leading off the glacier onto the east face here, then pick up the Class 3-4 ledges and heathery gully toward the summit block.
waypoints.directions: The finger rises off the top of the glacier and is steep enough that crampons and a second tool are the norm. A crevasse commonly cuts it partway up and has to be turned. Near the dark towers at its top, move off snow onto rock and round the corner east to reach the ledge system.

waypoints.name: Overcoat Peak
waypoints.note: True summit; the final ~400 vertical ft is a Class 4/low-5.0 heathery gully leading to an angled chimney, with a small summit register.
waypoints.directions: The gully has solid holds but a few tall steps force committing, exposed moves, and most parties pitch it out on small cams and nuts in mediocre rock rather than soloing it. Sort the descent before you commit: the damp dihedral below is normally rappelled twice, not downclimbed.

waypoints.name: North Fork Sauk Trailhead
waypoints.note: Northwest Forest Pass/self-issue wilderness permit at the kiosk; Red Mountain Trail #651 splits off ~100 yd down North Fork Sauk Trail #649.
waypoints.directions: From Darrington the drive is about 16 miles south on the Mountain Loop Highway to the North Fork Sauk River Road, then roughly 7.4 more miles to the Sloan Creek Campground lot.

waypoints.name: Red Mountain Trail #651 junction
waypoints.note: Signed fork off North Fork Sauk Trail #649 marked 'Painted Mountain Lookout trail 1 mile'; climbs via a couple of long switchbacks through old-growth.
waypoints.directions: The fork comes up almost immediately, about 100 yards along #649, and is low-key enough to walk straight past. If you have been on the main trail more than a couple of minutes you have missed it.

waypoints.name: Old lookout site overlook
waypoints.note: Flat bench where the 1936 fire lookout (destroyed 1967) once stood, with views into Pride Basin; maintained tread effectively ends here.
waypoints.directions: About a mile of steady switchbacking through old-growth on abandoned but well-trodden lookout tread, gaining roughly 700 feet. It is the last easy-to-follow section of the day.

waypoints.name: Exposed ledge scramble
waypoints.note: Steep dirt-covered rock with switchbacking ledges for about 70 vertical feet, Class 3 in a few spots — the crux, just past where tread ends.
waypoints.directions: The path keeps climbing steeply past the bench and the cliff band appears within a few hundred vertical feet; this is where most hikers turn around. Take the switchbacking line up the ledges rather than forcing the rock directly, and treat it as insecure when wet, since the holds carry dirt and moss rather than clean stone.

waypoints.name: Ruby Lake basin
waypoints.note: Small (~4-acre) tarn in the basin below Red Mountain's south side, reached via a faint boot path with occasional pink-ribbon flagging; the climber's route up the peak starts from the ledge above it.
waypoints.directions: Above the ledges the track thins to an intermittent boot path through steep open meadow, gaining around 2,700 feet along the crest and its southwest side. The route stays high above the water rather than dropping to the lake. The flagging is old and easily lost where the meadows open out, and the path effectively ends at the overlook, which is the key route-finding point of the day.

waypoints.name: Scree ridge above treeline
waypoints.note: Ground cover ends here — the final several hundred feet is loose scree and talus on the summit ridge; stay on the flagged boot path, especially in fog or on descent.
waypoints.directions: Keep climbing the ridge from the overlook rather than contouring into the basin below. It is several hundred feet of steep meadow and broken red-stained rock to where the last trees give out; note where you top out of the timber, because that spot is not obvious from above on the way down.

waypoints.name: Painted Mountain summit
waypoints.note: Broad red-rock summit (native name Ska-hala-bats) with views of Sloan Peak's glacier, Pride Basin, and south to Spring and Pugh.
waypoints.directions: The angle eases over the last stretch as the ridge broadens toward the summit dome. Footing rather than exposure is the issue here, and the whole climb runs around five hours from the car for a fit party.

waypoints.name: SR-20 Hairpin pullout (Kangaroo Temple / Spire Gully)
waypoints.note: Corrected - previous waypoints incorrectly placed this route ~137 miles away near Mount Rainier (a research error confusing an unrelated location with the real Ice Box formation). Ice Box is a Washington Pass roadside crag (Hairpin Crags), reached via a short trail/slab scramble above the highway's hairpin turn.

waypoints.name: Ice Box right side topout
waypoints.note: Ice Box right side topout at Hairpin Crags, Washington Pass; the neighbouring Ice Box left side crag holds Iceman, Route C and Route D.

waypoints.name: Luna Camp
waypoints.note: Established NPS backcountry campsite ~10 mi up the Big Beaver Trail (permit reserved at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center); base camp for leaving the maintained trail to find the Access/Luna Creek drainages.

waypoints.name: Luna Creek bushwhack
waypoints.note: Off-trail ascent from Luna Camp through devil's club and alder thickets; one of the worst bushwhacks in the North Cascades, and it's easy to lose the drainage in the brush.

waypoints.name: Crooked Thumb Glacier moraine high camp
waypoints.note: High camp on the glacier's lateral moraine per route beta; last reliable tent sites and meltwater before dropping toward Phantom Peak's southwest buttress.

waypoints.name: Southwest buttress saddle
waypoints.note: Gained via a roughly 1,000 ft descending traverse from the moraine camp; from here the route turns onto the pocket glacier on the buttress's southwest side.

waypoints.name: Bergschrund on the summit snow finger
waypoints.note: The pocket glacier's left-hand snow finger is cut by a bergschrund that's wide but shallow; parties crampon up slabby rock and crawl over the uphill wall to continue past it.

waypoints.name: Hannegan Pass Trailhead (end of Ruth Creek Rd / FR-32), via Hannegan Pass, Chilliwack River Trail, Whatcom Pass and Perfect Pass to the SW side of Phantom Peak
waypoints.note: This route is reached from the west side of the range over Hannegan Pass, not from Ross Lake.

waypoints.name: Phantom Peak summit (Southwest/South Route, Class 4, easiest route, FA Fred & Helmy Beckey 1940)
Reflection Lakes Trailhead
waypoints.note: South side of Stevens Canyon Road at the Reflection Lakes parking pullouts; Mount Rainier NP entrance fee applies, no water at the lot.
waypoints.directions: Park at the Reflection Lakes pullouts on Stevens Canyon Road, at about 4,860 ft. It is a small paved pullout lot and it fills early on weekends, so plan an early arrival. A Mount Rainier National Park entrance fee applies, and there is no water at the lot, so fill up before you get here. The trail is signed but unnumbered and starts directly across Stevens Canyon Road from the parking. When the road is snow-gated, winter parties start instead from the Narada Falls pullout.

waypoints.name: Seasonal Stream Crossing
waypoints.note: Small seasonal stream crosses the trail; often dry by late summer so don't rely on it for resupply.

waypoints.name: Cliff Bands Below Trail
waypoints.note: Trail runs directly beneath exposed cliff bands here; watch for rockfall and loose debris, especially if goats or other hikers are above.

waypoints.name: Pinnacle Saddle
waypoints.note: Maintained NPS trail ends at this 5,920-ft saddle between Pinnacle and Plummer Peaks; unmarked climber's path to the summit gully begins on the south side.

waypoints.name: Base of Summit Gully
waypoints.note: Climber's path traverses goat trails and loose scree around the peak's south side to reach the start of the class 3-4 ascent gully.

waypoints.name: Summit Gully Scramble
waypoints.note: NPS warns this is a precipitous scramble on loose, unstable rock; a few class 3 moves carry real exposure, so avoid climbing directly below other parties.

waypoints.name: Pinnacle Peak Summit
waypoints.note: True summit and second-highest point in the Tatoosh Range, with sweeping views of Rainier, Adams, and St. Helens.

waypoints.name: Westside Road / Dry Creek (Tahoma Creek) Trailhead
waypoints.note: End of driveable Westside Road (3.2 mi from the Nisqually-Longmire Rd junction), gated at Dry Creek. CHECK THIS BEFORE YOU DRIVE: the National Park Service's only two listed accesses to Indian Henry's Hunting Ground — the next waypoint on this route — are Kautz Creek (11.5 mi round trip) and Longmire (13 mi round trip). The Westside Road and Tahoma Creek corridor is not among them, and route beta for Success Cleaver reports the Tahoma Creek Trail closed for flood hazard, leaving Longmire via the Wonderland Trail as the standard approach. The mileages recorded on this route's waypoints are measured from this Dry Creek gate, so they describe the older corridor rather than a Longmire or Kautz Creek start — treat them as approximate if you approach from either of those, and confirm current trail status with a wilderness information centre.
waypoints.directions: Drive SR 706 to the Nisqually Entrance in the park's south-west corner; the road is paved and open essentially year round, conditions permitting. Westside Road leaves the Nisqually to Longmire road and is driveable about three miles to the gate at Dry Creek, where a standing, non-seasonal closure caused by repeated Tahoma Creek washouts stops vehicles; past the gate it is open to foot and bike traffic only. Longmire, where the nearest wilderness information centre is and where you register in and out, lies about 3.5 miles further along the main road.

waypoints.name: Indian Henry's Hunting Ground (patrol cabin)
waypoints.note: Historic 1915 patrol cabin marks where the route leaves the maintained Wonderland Trail for cross-country travel toward the Mirror Lakes basin.

waypoints.name: Mirror Lakes
waypoints.note: Small tarns about a mile off the Wonderland Trail; last dependable water before contouring dry southwest/west slopes of Pyramid Peak.
waypoints.directions: Leave the maintained Wonderland Trail at the patrol cabin and take the Mirror Lakes spur west, crossing marshy meadow on a series of plank walkways. Maintained tread ends part way along and the path fades into a boot track at about 5,600 ft, in the basin between Copper Peak and Pyramid Peak, roughly a mile off the Wonderland. These tarns are the last dependable water before the dry south-west and west slopes of Pyramid Peak.

waypoints.name: Point 6631 (base camp north of Pyramid Peak)
waypoints.note: Flat campsites just north of this 6,631 ft high point give broad views of Success Cleaver; position is estimated, not surveyed — interpolated along the contour around Pyramid Peak.
waypoints.directions: From the tarns it is cross-country travel. Head north-east out of the basin and contour the south-west then west slopes of Pyramid Peak, staying roughly between 6,000 and 6,300 ft, to reach Point 6631 just north of the peak. There is no boot-pack and only sparse cairning through here, so carry a map or GPS track and expect to find your own line; snowmelt water is often available around the point into early summer, and the rock-slab camp below Pyramid Peak near 6,300 ft is a common first night.

waypoints.name: 6,400 ft saddle below Success Cleaver
waypoints.note: Short descent NNE from Point 6631 to this saddle; typical high camp before scrambling onto the lower cleaver at first light.
waypoints.directions: Drop north-north-east from Point 6631 a short way to the saddle at about 6,400 ft, which is the start of Success Cleaver proper. It is a scree and loose-boulder col and it looks unpleasant, which is how you know it is the right place. There is an easier way down into it than the obvious line, and parties record missing it and taking the worst ground, so pick the descent out before you commit and note it for the return.

waypoints.name: Lower Success Cleaver gendarmes
waypoints.note: Loose rock towers force weaving route-finding on the lower rib; rockfall risk climbs if other parties are above; bivy options around 8,100-8,300 ft.
waypoints.directions: From the col the cleaver rises straight ahead and does not let up: loose choss and scree with short bursts of class 3 scrambling, no track and no cairned line, weaving among rock towers on ground you route-find yourself. Use what is on either side as the test. The South Tahoma Glacier should fall away to climber's left and the Pyramid and Success glaciers to climber's right; if you find yourself on a glacier, or if the going out of the col is pleasant walking on solid rock, you have drifted off the cleaver and are contouring around Pyramid Peak instead. Rockfall risk rises sharply with any party above you, the rock firms up above roughly 7,000 ft, and there are bivy sites around 8,100 to 8,300 ft.

waypoints.name: Rockfall chutes to Kautz Cleaver headwall
waypoints.note: Angle across three loose, rockfall-swept chutes to the headwall and gain the Kautz Cleaver near 12,600 ft; helmet mandatory, best crossed before sun loosens rock.
waypoints.directions: Follow the cleaver crest up through class 3 and short class 4 rock bands and steep chutes, past bivy benches near 9,400 ft and the small col at about 10,700 ft. Higher, the crest holds a knife-edge section that needs genuine scrambling once the snow has melted off it, and the route then angles climber's right up snow gullies and across three loose, rockfall-swept chutes to the headwall, joining the Kautz Cleaver between roughly 12,200 and 12,600 ft. Cross those chutes early, before the sun starts releasing rock and ice; helmets on.

waypoints.name: Point Success
waypoints.directions: From the Kautz Cleaver climb steepening snow and ice, generally around 45 degrees, to the headwall below the summit. A cliff band bars the way and is passed either by a short low fifth class rock step, exposed and sometimes wet or icy, or by an isolated snow and ice pitch of about 15 ft at up to 55 degrees, depending on the season. Above it the angle eases onto the summit plateau at Point Success, 14,158 ft.

waypoints.name: Thirtymile Trailhead
waypoints.note: From here, follow Chewuch River Trail #510 to Remmel Lake, then go off-trail south (~2 miles bushwhack) to reach the NW Ridge; this is the line of the 2011 ascent.

waypoints.name: Four Point Lake
waypoints.note: Multiple good campsites with views of Remmel; standard bivy.

waypoints.name: NW Ridge Camp
waypoints.note: Bivy on Remmel's NW Ridge itself, reached via ridge travel from the Four Point Lake basin.

waypoints.name: Boston Basin Trailhead (Cascade River Road pullout)
waypoints.note: Unmarked pullout at mile ~22 of Cascade River Road opposite Johannesburg Mountain, room for 6-8 cars; self-issue wilderness permit and Northwest Forest Pass required.
waypoints.directions: The Boston Basin start is an unmarked climbers' pullout on Cascade River Road, about 21.7 miles from Marblemount at roughly 3,200-3,300 ft, sitting opposite Johannesburg Mountain. There is no trailhead sign of any kind, so watch your odometer rather than looking for signage — it is easy to drive straight past. The pullout holds six to eight cars and you need a Northwest Forest Pass to park. Camping in Boston Basin needs a North Cascades wilderness permit picked up in person at Marblemount, and the popular sites fill fast in the early-access lottery for peak summer weekends.

waypoints.name: Creek crossings through old-growth forest
waypoints.note: Climbers' path follows an old mining road then crosses several small streams in old-growth timber before switchbacking to treeline; reliable water but poorly marked in low light.

waypoints.name: Boston Basin low camp
waypoints.note: Designated moraine campsite with composting toilet at treeline; most parties continue higher for a shorter summit day.

waypoints.name: Boston Basin high camp
waypoints.note: Upper hardened camp on slabs/grass below Sharkfin Tower, closer to the Quien Sabe Glacier; the informal camps below Sharkfin are on this bench.

waypoints.name: Glacier rope-up point beneath Sharkfin Tower
waypoints.note: Where the boot path meets continuous snow on the Quien Sabe Glacier's lower-angle (north/left) side; rope up for crevasses here.

waypoints.name: Bergschrund crossing
waypoints.note: Narrow snow bridge crosses above and left of the bergschrund late-season; crevasses widen through August-September and the crossing point shifts year to year.

waypoints.name: Boston-Sahale Col
waypoints.note: Top of the glacier traverse beneath the Sharkfin face; gains the col between Sahale and Boston Peak before the final scramble.

waypoints.name: Sahale Mountain summit
waypoints.note: Short, exposed 3rd/4th-class scramble up the summit block from the col; the true summit block has fixed anchors used by many parties to rappel back to the col.

waypoints.name: Downey Creek Trailhead
waypoints.note: Northwest Forest Pass required; parking lot is just past the Downey Creek bridge on Suiattle River Road (FR 26), about 20 mi from Hwy 530.
waypoints.directions: Drive Suiattle River Road (FR 26) about 20 miles in from Highway 530; the parking area sits just past the Downey Creek bridge at roughly 1,450 feet. Display a Northwest Forest Pass. Check the road before you commit to the trip, because it is frequently washed out or gated well short of the trailhead, adding miles of walking or biking each way that none of the trail mileage here accounts for. The route is normally in condition July through September.

waypoints.name: Sixmile Camp
waypoints.note: Established camp along the easy, flat Downey Creek Trail #768 where the route leaves the maintained trail and turns east along Bachelor Creek.
waypoints.directions: Follow Downey Creek Trail #768 for 6.5 miles from the trailhead — easy, well-graded and mostly flat through forest, with a suspension-bridge crossing of Downey Creek.

waypoints.name: Bachelor Creek crossing
waypoints.note: Ford or log-cross Bachelor Creek to its south side here; the climbers' path above is badly overgrown with slide alder up to roughly 4,400 ft.
waypoints.directions: The maintained trail ends here; continue on the unmaintained Bachelor Creek climbers' path, staying on the north side of the creek at first, then ford to the south side at about the 9.5-mile mark. Treat it as a real creek crossing — harder and more dangerous in high water or early season.

waypoints.name: Cub Lake Pass
waypoints.note: Gap on the ridge crest northwest of Cub Lake (~5,880 ft), gained by switchbacks; begin the ~500 ft descent to the lake basin from here.
waypoints.directions: Climb the climbers' path above the crossing. Near 4,500 ft the tread largely disappears through a large avalanche-debris zone, so expect slow, brushy route-finding through slide alder and downed timber; above the debris the path climbs to the pass on the ridge crest northwest of Cub Lake.

waypoints.name: Cub Lake
waypoints.note: High camp with reliable water at the lake basin; Itswoot Ridge, reached by traversing further, is the alternate camp some parties use instead.
waypoints.directions: Drop about 500 ft off the pass into the lake basin. These are snow slopes into midsummer and this is normally the crux navigation of the approach day when they are covered.

waypoints.name: Dome Glacier crossing
waypoints.note: Cross the Dome Glacier's crevasses toward the Dome-Sinister col; a bergschrund spans the glacier and requires finding a solid snowbridge.
waypoints.directions: Most parties push on from the lake basin up onto Itswoot Ridge for high camp, then traverse climbers' paths and snow benches through the upper basins, staying near 7,000 ft, to gain the glacier. Rope up for glacier travel and carry crevasse-rescue gear before starting across.

waypoints.name: Dome-Sinister col
waypoints.note: Saddle between Dome and Sinister Peaks; from here contour on an easy snowfield around to Sinister's south side to reach the loose southwest gully.
waypoints.directions: Cross over the Dome–Chikamin col and descend the crevassed Chikamin Glacier to about 7,200 ft, then traverse right (east) across the glacier to the col. The bergschrund guarding it can be hard to cross in late season and has sometimes required a short rappel to get down onto or across it.

waypoints.name: Sinister Peak
waypoints.note: True summit, just under a mile east of Dome Peak along the connecting ridge; reached via the loose southwest gully to the upper west ridge.
waypoints.directions: From the col contour around on an easy snowfield to Sinister's south side, then climb the loose, unpleasant gully to gain the upper west ridge and scramble Class 2–3 along the ridge to the top. Loose rock in the gully is the main hazard — move fast and keep the party out of each other's fall line; some parties skip it and take the exposed Class 3+ ridge directly from the col.

waypoints.name: Elbow Lake Trail - North Trailhead (FR 38)
waypoints.note: Low-elevation trailhead off FR 38 via Mosquito Lake Rd; Northwest Forest Pass required, and FR 38 is gated Dec 1-Jun 15 at Wallace Creek. This is a separate trailhead from 'Pioneer Camp,' which sits at the trail's south end off Baker Lake Highway/FSR 12.
waypoints.directions: From the Mount Baker Ranger District office in Sedro-Woolley, drive north on WA-9 to Acme and turn right (east) onto Mosquito Lake Road for about 9 miles, crossing the Middle Fork Nooksack River, then continue onto Forest Road 38 for roughly 11 miles to the north trailhead for the Elbow Lake Trail at about 2,000 feet. A Northwest Forest Pass is required, and FR 38 is gated at Wallace Creek from December 1 through June 15. Do not confuse this with the Pioneer Camp trailhead, which sits at the trail's south end off the Baker Lake Highway (FSR 12). As of mid-2026 FR 38 was damaged in the December 2025 floods with no published repair date, so confirm current road conditions with the Mount Baker Ranger District before you drive in.

waypoints.name: Middle Fork Nooksack River crossing
waypoints.note: No bridge on this side — cross via an unofficial log/rope rig a few hundred yards up or downstream; can be unfordable at high flow, and the log has washed out in past seasons.

waypoints.name: Green Creek climbers' path junction (Hildebrand Creek switchback)
waypoints.note: Unmaintained, sparsely blue-blazed climbers' trail for Green Creek Cirque splits off the maintained Elbow Lake Trail #697 at a switchback near Hildebrand Creek — easy to walk past, watch for paint blazes and flagging.

waypoints.name: Green Creek at the cirque mouth
waypoints.note: Green Creek runs clear here at the entrance to the Green Creek Cirque — treat this as the last reliable water before the upper slabs and summit ridge.

waypoints.name: Connecting ridge gain point south of South Twin
waypoints.note: Loose, engaging 3rd/4th-class scrambling out of the cirque gains the ridge crest just south of South Twin; from here the route turns south along the connecting ridge to Skookum on grippy olivine.

waypoints.name: Skookum Peak summit
waypoints.note: True summit (also known as 'Kloke Peak'); descend by reversing the ridge and climbers' path back to the Green Creek Cirque.

waypoints.name: Stevens Pass North Lot Trailhead
waypoints.note: Park in the large lot on the north side of US-2 at Stevens Pass; start near the small gray/red building and follow the gravel service road to its left - no parking fee or permit required.

waypoints.name: Service Road Y-Junction (5,050 ft)
waypoints.note: Service road flattens and forks here; leave the road and cut northwest on the climbers' path toward Skyline Lake rather than continuing straight.

waypoints.name: Skyline Lake
waypoints.note: Trail skirts the lake's south shore; reliable water source and a popular winter camp for scout groups, but freezes over and can be walked across in snow season.

waypoints.name: Ridge Gap NW of Skyline Lake
waypoints.note: Gain the gap on the Skyline/Heather Ridge crest just northwest of the lake - about 100 ft of extra climbing opens the first views north; this is where the route leaves the lake basin for the ridge. Coordinate is a geometric interpolation along the ridge bearing between Skyline Lake and the summit, estimated and not independently verified.

waypoints.name: Rocky Sub-Summit Traverse
waypoints.note: Route traverses below several loose, rocky high points on the undulating ridge crest; a few of the slopes here can slide in winter/spring snow, and most casual hikers turn back at the lower rocky sub-summit. Coordinate is a geometric interpolation along the ridge bearing between Skyline Lake and the summit, estimated and not independently verified.

waypoints.name: Sky Mountain Summit
waypoints.note: True summit at the end of the Skyline/Heather Ridge crest; only a faint climbers' path reaches it, with views to Tye Peak, Cowboy Mountain, and the Stevens Pass basin.

waypoints.name: Index-Galena Road / North Fork Skykomish River Access (FR-63, ~Mile 10)
waypoints.note: Park at the snowplow turnaround by the bridge about 1 mile east of Galena; this is the last reliable water, none is found once you leave the road.
waypoints.directions: Drive US 2 to Skykomish, then head north on the Beckler River Road (FR-65) for about 15 miles and turn right (east) onto FR-63. A high-clearance vehicle is worth having for the last few miles. Park at the turnaround by the river crossing near Galena at about 1,150 feet; the pullout is unmarked and easy to drive past. No permits are needed, and the river here is the last dependable water, since there is none once you leave the road.

waypoints.name: Old Logging Road / 2300-ft Saddle
waypoints.note: After a steep, brush-free first 600 ft through downed timber, cross an old overgrown logging road at this saddle on the lower north slopes.

waypoints.name: Hogsback Ridge Top
waypoints.note: The well-defined hogsback you've been following since ~2700 ft terminates here; continue straight uphill toward the cliff bands above.

waypoints.name: Cliff Band Traverse
waypoints.note: Large cliff bands block the north end of the peak between roughly 4200-4400 ft; traverse southeast below them to reach the mountain's west/northwest side.

waypoints.name: 5940-ft Saddle Northwest of Summit
waypoints.note: Gain this saddle via the traverse; a possible schrund/moat forms here depending on season and snow cover before you turn onto the final ridge.

waypoints.name: Class 5 Step
waypoints.note: The final ridge is mostly Class 3, but two short sections here are Class 4-5; many parties place a rope for this exposed step.

waypoints.name: Spire Mountain
waypoints.note: True summit at the top of the west/northwest ridge scramble, with views over the Monte Cristo peaks and North Fork Skykomish valley.

waypoints.name: Pete Lake Trailhead
waypoints.note: Self-issue wilderness permit required at the kiosk; Northwest Forest Pass or $5 day-use fee for parking (Cooper Lake Rd / FR-46).

waypoints.name: PCT junction near Lemah Meadow
waypoints.note: Climbers' bypass leaves the Pete Lake Trail/PCT corridor here near 4,000 ft, cutting the Lemah Meadow dogleg to save ~3 miles.

waypoints.name: Vista Lakes (upper lake)
waypoints.note: Established high camp at the upper Vista Lake tarn; warm swimming water and the standard bivy for a summit push.

waypoints.name: Point 5965 / Summit Chief Pass
waypoints.note: Climb easy terrain west of Vista Lakes over Pt. 5965, then drop to Summit Chief Pass and pick up the ridge running northwest toward the peak.

waypoints.name: Summit Chief Lake talus basin
waypoints.note: Lower talus basin by a snowfield below Summit Chief Lake; common spot to stash packs before the final climb.

waypoints.name: Moat / icy entry gully
waypoints.note: A moat here can be trip-ending after mid-July or in low-snow years; the adjoining gully is often icy in the morning, so carry crampons.

waypoints.name: Notch in the south ridge skyline
waypoints.note: Small notch gained by a rising talus traverse; this is the turnaround/gear-swap point for the final loose gully to the top.

waypoints.name: Summit Chief Mountain (true summit)
waypoints.note: True summit on the King/Kittitas county line, 9 miles NE of Snoqualmie Pass; descend by reversing the loose upper gully and steep dirt to the ridge notch.

waypoints.name: Foggy Dew Trailhead (FR 4340-200, Trail #417)
waypoints.note: Coordinate and elevation as published by the Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest for the Foggy Dew Trailhead, where Foggy Dew Trail #417 begins. This REPLACES a pin that was actually the Eagle Lakes / Crater Creek trailhead (4,740 ft, ~2.9 mi away): Eagle Lakes Trail #431 runs to Martin and Cooney Lakes and never passes Foggy Dew Falls, which is the next waypoint here. Every recorded distance on this route is consistent with this trailhead and impossible from the other.

waypoints.name: Foggy Dew Falls
waypoints.note: Steep switchback section passes a two-tiered cascade in a narrow cleft; last easy, reliable water before the trail breaks into open basin country.

waypoints.name: Merchants Basin / Cooney Lake Trail #434 split
waypoints.note: Trail #417 tops out of timber into the open, wildflower-covered Merchants Basin below Sawtooth Ridge, where the Cooney Lake Trail #434 splits off toward Cooney Lake.

waypoints.name: Cooney Lake
waypoints.note: Larch-rimmed alpine lake with established camps near the outlet; last reliable water before climbing to the pass.

waypoints.name: Cooney Pass
waypoints.note: 7,900 ft saddle on Switchback's southeast side gains the crest of the Southeast Ridge, with views down into Merchants Basin and toward Sunrise Lake.

waypoints.name: Southeast Ridge scramble
waypoints.note: Class 2-3 rock scramble up loose, exposed talus/blocks on the ridge crest to the summit block; expect strong, cold wind near the top.

waypoints.name: Barclay Creek crossing / leave trail
waypoints.note: About a quarter mile past the trailhead, cross Barclay Creek on a stout logjam ~200 yards upstream of an old spur road, then bushwhack toward an overgrown corrugated culvert marking the start of the Tailgunner climbers' path.

waypoints.name: Rocky knob on climbers' path
waypoints.note: Old logging-road tread gives way to a rockier, more open knob roughly 2.8 hours up from the trailhead; route-finding gets easier here as the path steepens into Tailgunner Ravine. The knob sits at ~3,600 ft; position is estimated, not surveyed.

waypoints.name: Waterfall ravine
waypoints.note: The 'infamous waterfall ravine' cliff band at ~4,000 ft: a Class 2-3 scramble around a waterfall in the ravine that forces a short descent and re-ascent; slick rock when wet. Position is estimated, not surveyed.

waypoints.name: Brushy cliff-band weakness
waypoints.note: Leave the Tailgunner Couloir here through a brushy weakness in the cliff band to gain the crest of the west ridge; grassy slopes and firm snow patches persist into early summer. Position is estimated, not surveyed.

waypoints.name: Tailgunner Pass
waypoints.note: Broad saddle between Gunn Point and Tailgunner reached after ~3,000 ft of gain; couloir approach and the upper Gunn Basin camps converge here. Position is estimated, not surveyed.

waypoints.name: West ridge gendarmes / cornice headwall
waypoints.note: Follow the ridge crest over minor gendarmes; a relic cornice headwall near the summit dome requires careful, exposed scrambling, especially with lingering snow. Position is estimated, not surveyed.

waypoints.name: Barclay Lake Trailhead (FR-6024)
waypoints.note: End of FR-6024 (Barclay Creek Road); shared trailhead for Barclay Lake, Gunn Peak, Gunn Point, Tailgunner, and Wing Peak approaches via Barclay Creek and Tailgunner Pass.

waypoints.name: Goodell Creek Trailhead
waypoints.note: Old Goodell Creek logging road on SR 20 across from Newhalem Campground; free NPS backcountry permit required for any overnight camping in North Cascades National Park.
waypoints.directions: Drive SR-20 to Newhalem. Coming from the west through Marblemount and Concrete the road is open year-round, since the seasonal highway closure gate sits farther east near Ross Dam and Diablo. Park at the Goodell Creek trailhead on the north side of SR-20, across from Newhalem Campground: take the left just past the Goodell Creek crossing, continue past the gravel pit, and follow the road to its end by the creek at about 500 ft. Any overnight camping in North Cascades National Park needs a free backcountry wilderness permit, and the Crescent/Terror Creek approach is usually not snow-free and reliably passable until mid-to-late July.

waypoints.name: Climbers' Path Cairn
waypoints.note: Cairn marking where the unmaintained Terror Basin/Barrier climbers' path leaves the overgrown Goodell Creek roadbed and turns steeply uphill toward the Southern Pickets.

waypoints.name: Terror Creek Log Crossing
waypoints.note: Cross Terror Creek on a large logjam ford point used by climbers approaching the Barrier; can be slick and the log position shifts year to year.

waypoints.name: The Barrier Crest
waypoints.note: Small saddle atop a notoriously loose class-3 ridge dividing the Terror and Crescent Creek basins; careful route-finding and rockfall awareness needed here.

waypoints.name: Stump Hollow
waypoints.note: Open, gentle slabby/heather basin between the Barrier and Chopping Block ridge — the standard high camp for the South Route.

waypoints.name: South Face Gully
waypoints.note: Loose gully on the south side of the Chopping Block/Barrier ridge gains the sloping south face; helmet on, watch for rockfall onto climbers below.

waypoints.name: The Chopping Block
waypoints.note: True summit (6,819 ft), labeled Pinnacle Peak on USGS maps; visible from the North Cascades NP Newhalem visitor center on clear days.

waypoints.name: Snow Lakes Trailhead
waypoints.note: Trailhead parking lot on Icicle Creek Road, 4.2-4.3 mi from the US-2/Icicle Creek Road junction.
waypoints.directions: Follow Icicle Creek Road to its end, about 4.3 miles from US-2, to reach the Snow Lakes trailhead at roughly 1,300 feet. Park at the trailhead and cross Icicle Creek on the trail bridge to pick up Snow Lakes Trail No. 1553. If you plan to camp overnight in the Enchantments Core Zone near Temple Canyon, a lottery-based overnight permit is required; without one, most parties either climb it car-to-car in one long day or camp outside the Core Zone near Nada Lake.

waypoints.name: Saddle Lake / Three Fingers Trailhead (Trail #641)
waypoints.note: Trailhead on Tupso Pass Spur Rd (FR 4160) off FR 41; no permit required, but the access road has a permanent washout past the Canyon Creek bridge that adds miles of foot/bike travel to reach here.

waypoints.name: Saddle Lake
waypoints.note: Soggy subalpine lake with an Everett Mountaineers-built shelter at its meadow edge; camping is banned within 200 ft of the lake and campfires are prohibited from here upward.
waypoints.directions: Follow Trail #641 uphill from the parking area on a steady forest grade, crossing a couple of small seasonal streams on the way. Routefinding is straightforward and the lake arrives as an abrupt soggy opening rather than a viewpoint. Fill bottles here, since this is the last easy water before the alpine part of the route.

waypoints.name: Goat Flats
waypoints.note: Broad open meadow atop the ridge and the standard basecamp for the climb, about 2.5 mi below the lookout; reliable snowmelt tarns nearby but can dry out late season.
waypoints.directions: Climb roughly two more miles past the lake, gaining out of the timber and onto the crest of the ridge before the trail opens into subalpine meadow with views west toward Puget Sound. Campfires are prohibited from the lake upward, so plan a stove-only camp when you stop.

waypoints.name: Tin Can Gap
waypoints.note: Trail crisscrosses the ridge to gain this notch; marks the end of maintained tread and the start of technical scrambling toward the peaks.
waypoints.directions: From the meadows the trail contours and climbs about two more miles, crisscrossing the ridge crest as it works north. Snow lies across this stretch well into summer and can bury the tread entirely, so carry an axe and expect to navigate by terrain rather than by trail. The gap gives the first full view of the three summits and the glacier below; do not continue past it without snow gear and routefinding experience, as this is where parties have needed rescue.

waypoints.name: South Peak lookout ladders
waypoints.note: Three wooden ladders rebarred and wired into the rock climb past the South Peak lookout pinnacle; exposed and can be icy early season, and this is the section the descent text means by 'downclimb the ladders.'
waypoints.directions: Leave the maintained trail and drop roughly 400 feet off the far side of the gap on snow or talus onto the upper glacier, then traverse and climb back up to the saddle beneath the South Peak lookout pinnacle. Early in the year this is a straightforward snow descent and re-ascent; later it goes to bare ice with a moat where the snow has pulled away from the rock, and getting on and off the ice is the awkward part. The ladders start from the rock immediately above that saddle.

waypoints.name: Queest-Alb Glacier headwall crossing
waypoints.note: Route drops onto the north side of the ridge near the top of the Queest-Alb Glacier; a slip on the icy headwall runs out toward crevasses lower on the glacier.
waypoints.directions: Continuing to the true summit means leaving the lookout and dropping back off the ridge onto the north side of the glacier, generally by a gully and rocky moraine rather than straight down. Rope up and watch the runout: the slope above the crevassed lower glacier holds ice by late season and a slip does not stop on its own. Most parties turn around at the lookout, so expect no boot track from here on.

waypoints.name: Col between Middle and North Finger
waypoints.note: Traverse across the glacier gains this col between the Middle and North Fingers, the jump-off point for the West Couloir onto North Peak's South Face.
waypoints.directions: Traverse north across the glacier below the Middle Finger, then climb roughly a thousand feet of snow to the notch; the eastern of the gullies leading up takes steps well when it is firm. Crampons and an axe are wanted, and small crevasses open along the traverse as the season goes on. The col is the last flat ground, so sort gear there before starting up the rock.

waypoints.name: North Peak, Three Fingers
waypoints.note: True summit (Class 4, 5.4 variation), topped out via the West Couloir and South Face above the col; descend by reversing the snow slopes, trail, and ladders.
waypoints.directions: From the col climb the West Couloir onto the South Face, starting on loose third and fourth class rock where anyone above will send debris down. Follow the ramp on the ridge to a chimney holding the hardest moves, exposed fourth to low fifth class and worth a rope and a few slings; a direct line on the upper west face is harder still at about 5.4. Above the chimney the angle eases to class 2-3, but a false summit sits short of the real one, so keep going until you find the register. Coming down is two to three rappels through the chimney and ramp section, often off fixed slings of unknown age that should be backed up.

waypoints.name: Tomyhoi Lake / Yellow Aster Butte Trailhead
waypoints.note: End of FR 3065 (Twin Lakes Road), 4.5 mi off SR 542; Northwest Forest Pass required and roadside parking along the switchbacks is very limited.

waypoints.name: Gold Run Pass
waypoints.note: Trail forks near the pass: right drops to Tomyhoi Lake, route stays left toward Yellow Aster Butte meadows.
waypoints.directions: Start on the Yellow Aster Butte trail and climb steeply — roughly 1,500 ft in the first mile and a half — through an avalanche path and then forest, crossing a couple of small seasonal creeks low down that are the easiest water on the route early in the season. At the signed fork the right branch carries on over the pass and down to Tomyhoi Lake; stay left for the Yellow Aster meadows.

waypoints.name: Yellow Aster tarns / meadows
waypoints.note: High plateau of small glacier-carved tarns; all camping must be at or beyond this point (LNT-only, camp on snow/rock/bare ground, not the fragile meadow turf) — reliable water from the tarns.
waypoints.directions: Beyond the fork the grade eases and the trail traverses the south flank of the butte for a bit over two miles as the terrain opens into meadow. At an unsigned junction around three and a half miles the path to the butte's summit goes right; drop left instead on narrow, steep switchbacks into the tarn basin.

waypoints.name: Boot path onto Tomyhoi Arm
waypoints.note: Leave the maintained trail here and pick up the well-defined climbers' boot path heading north along the crest of Tomyhoi Arm toward the southeast ridge.
waypoints.directions: Leave the maintained trail at the basin and head north-northwest, over a broad hump and down to a col near 6,270 ft, where a well-beaten climbers' boot path picks up along the crest. Getting onto the right crest is the thing to be careful about here — the arm runs north toward the peak, and the trail system does not go that way.

waypoints.name: Moat below Tomyhoi Glacier remnant
waypoints.note: Shallow moat/hard snow between rock and the shrinking glacier remnant — usually the crux; carry an ice axe, and it can be bypassed 100-200 ft lower via a rock finger if snow is firm.
waypoints.directions: Follow the boot path up the broadening ridge, and where the crest narrows above roughly 6,800 ft drop onto the broad benches on the north side rather than staying on top. The path fades into scree and talus as you near the toe of the glacier remnant; traverse along its upper edge to get past several rock pinnacles, assessing the ice before committing to it. Cross the moat between rock and ice — it is hard snow more often than not, which is why an axe belongs on this route, and if it is too firm it can be turned a hundred feet or two lower on a finger of rock.

waypoints.name: Notch below the false summit
waypoints.note: Gain this notch via a V-shaped Class 3.5 slot (some parties belay it), then traverse a ledge west to a wide corner leading up to the false summit.
waypoints.directions: Above the moat, gain the notch through a V-shaped slot of about Class 3.5. It is short but steep and exposed enough that parties often put a rope on it, and it is distinctly harder to reverse than to climb. From the notch, traverse a ledge west to the wide corner that leads up to the false summit.

waypoints.name: Tomyhoi Peak
waypoints.note: Class 3 scramble on solid rock from the false summit to the true summit block; sweeping views of Mt. Baker, Mt. Shuksan, and north into Canada.
waypoints.directions: From the false summit the true summit looks worse than it is. Downclimb loose ledges to the col between the two, then scramble the summit block on solid, glacier-polished rock — Class 3, with a short gabled section of ridge where the exposure is real on both sides.
